Hello, I've wired a 4-20mA analog sensor to my [product_name] using [article_no] and an [article_no] expansion module. On the [product_name] web interface, I see a value labeled '202' in the attached image. My sensor is connected to AI1, but I'm not sure what the 202 represents—is there a scale or conversion that should be applied to the analog input, or should scaling be performed on a remote server? Thank you, Best regards, [user_name]

Assuming you are referring to the topic about retrieving analog values from the expansion module: Without knowing the physical measuring range of your sensor connected to AI1, it's not possible to interpret the displayed values definitively. The [product_name] converts each analog input to a value between 0 and 1000 units, regardless if it’s a 0-10V, 0/4-20mA, or PT100/1000 input. For 4-20mA sensors, only 800 units are usable—the first 200 units correspond to the 4mA lower limit. Therefore, in your case, the AI1 value of 202 suggests the sensor’s measured value is near the minimum. You should scale the analog input to match the physical measurement range of your sensor using an analog amplifier.

Refer to this FAQ from [company_name]: How do you scale measured values in [product_name] Soft Comfort? For further guidance, consult the official documentation or knowledge base.

Hello everyone, I've been using the new webserver on the latest [product_name] recently. It works perfectly on my home network, but I'm unsure how to monitor the [product_name] from the internet. Any advice?

To enable remote access to your [product_name], you first need to open the correct port on your firewall or router so incoming internet connections can reach your internal network. By default, routers and firewalls block these connections. If you are on a corporate network, your IT team should handle this. The following steps assume a home network setup: Web browsers usually use port 80, but you can configure your firewall or router to map any external port to the internal port that your [product_name] is set up to receive requests from. For multiple [product_name] devices, assign unique port numbers so the router can direct the requests correctly. In practice, connect using the router's IP address, not the [product_name]'s internal IP. The documentation claims port 8080 is the one [product_name] listens on, but in my experience, opening port 80 internally was required. Not sure why [company_name] specifies 8080; perhaps someone else can explain. You'll either need a fixed IP from your ISP, or use a dynamic DNS (DDNS) service because your router's external IP can change. DDNS gives you a constant domain name, like [url], which you use to access the network. Set fixed IP addresses for each [product_name] device so your router forwards requests properly. After these steps, remote monitoring should work; I'm able to monitor mine over the internet at remote locations. In some cases, I have connected devices wirelessly when Ethernet cabling is not practical. If you're not on a home network, your IT department is the appropriate contact for these changes. Hope this is useful.

The main problem is the version difference between the panel's operating system and your project. Your HMI has Image version 15.1.0.0, and your [product_name] project has Image version 16.0.0.0. You have two options: 1) Swap the image version in [product_name] (see attached video), or 2) Update the operating system of your panel (refer to [url]). There are also issues in your tag table: you’ve defined variables from the [product_name] module as 'Word', but the correct data type is 'Int'. 'Word' refers to the data width (two bytes/16 bits), but for analog values, 'Int' is used (-32,768 to 32,767). In [product_name], a word is unsigned (0 to 65535), while an Int is signed (-32,768 to 32,767). Also, make sure the display formats in your I/O fields match the 'Int' data type.

Regarding option 2 for the HMI issue: upgrade the device to V16. It may take some time to update, but you'll get the latest features.

For scaling in [product_name] software: set up an analog amplifier block with 4-20 mA sensor, for temperature (min -40, max +60) and humidity (min 0, max 100). Using a 220 Ohm resistor results in a sensor span that is approximately 2.7 times higher than with 500 Ohm. With 220 Ohms, scale temp: min -40, max +233; for humidity: min 0, max 270 in [product_name] software.

The use of 200 Ohm resistors is incorrect; you should use 500 Ohm instead. For proper scaling instructions, see attached [document].

Hello, I am having trouble downloading over Ethernet to the [product_name] with [version_no]. The system displays the message: "can't access IP ***.***.*.* ". I've set my laptop to a static IP of 192.168.10.3 and the device to 192.168.10.2. Pinging the device via CMD returns a reply. What does this actually indicate?

Hi, did you manage to resolve your issue? I am encountering the same problem.

Could you provide more details? Are you connecting to the [product_name] directly or through a router? Which IPs do you assign for the device and your PC or laptop? Are these dedicated IP addresses?

I learned a few things about connecting to a controller via Ethernet: 1. Connect the controller directly to your PC's Ethernet port with a cable. 2. Disable other Ethernet connections like USB adapters and Wi-Fi, keeping only the one you use for the controller. 3. Assign a fixed IP address to the PC’s Ethernet port for initial setup. If it works and you usually use DHCP, enable DHCP and add an alternative IP in your settings. To activate the alternative IP, unplug and replug the Ethernet cable. 4. Run [product_name] programming software as Admin. If these steps are successful, you can then integrate the controller into your network to help pinpoint issues.

From my experience, the most reliable connection is to use an Ethernet cable to directly link your PC and the [product_name]. Avoid using networks with Wi-Fi or gateways, as unknown device IP addresses can cause conflicts. For example: 1. Device fresh from box. 2. Connected to a Wi-Fi router via Ethernet with default settings. 3. PC or laptop uses DHCP on Wi-Fi. Typically, issues arise because both the device and many routers default to IP 192.168.0.1. If you ping the device, the router may respond instead, making you think you’re connecting to the device when it’s actually the router. In this situation, the programming software cannot find the device. Also, always run the configuration software as Admin; Windows security may block it from adjusting network settings otherwise. Hope this helps.

Hi [user_name], you cannot change the actual program from the TD display—only parameters can be adjusted. If you want to prevent the operator from modifying a parameter, enable 'protection active' in the relevant function block. For example, if an on-delay timer is used, operators can change the time from the TD unless the 'protection active' option is enabled. If it is checked, operators cannot view or modify this parameter from the display.

Hello everyone, Does anyone know how to implement value comparisons (greater than, less than, or equal to) in a PLC? Looking forward to your responses! Best regards, [user_name]

Hi, You can use an analog comparator block for this purpose. By configuring two comparators with inverted inputs (A,B and B,A) and setting the threshold to zero: - When A > B, the first output is activated - When A < B, the second output is activated - When A = B, both outputs remain off Hope this helps!

Hello, every time there is a power outage on [product_name], the analog values stored with analog flags reset to zero. Is there a way to prevent this or work around the issue?

Could you share more details about how you use the analog flags? Please upload your program. Keep in mind that analog flags do not provide retentivity.

Thank you for your response. We use analog flags to set values like set points and orders through the web browser, so operators can update them easily. This setup works well until a power loss, at which point all values reset to zero. Any suggestions to resolve this issue are appreciated. Thanks in advance for your assistance.

The core issue is that analog flags lack retentive storage. You can try writing values via parameter VM mapping into the parameter of a mathematical instruction. This way, the data is saved in flash memory.

Hello, thank you for your advice. I tried your suggestion but couldn't get it to work. I've attached a sample diagram for reference—perhaps I made a mistake. If you could kindly check it, I would appreciate it. Thanks so much.

It would be more helpful to provide the [product_name] file in zip format instead of images. With your example, it's unclear how values are entered for retentive storage. See the attached example for the usual method: values from arithmetic blocks are mapped to the VM memory area, which you can modify via the extended webserver or a networked [product_name]. Analog flags are unsuitable for storing values; only block parameters (timers, analog, etc.) should be used. Regards, [user_name]

Hello [user_name], in your example, retentive storage doesn't work because you are writing by reference instead of directly into the arithmetic instruction parameter via parameter VM mapping. Referenced values won't be retained for mathematical instruction parameters.

However, the attached image shows that the Modbus address space in [product_name] covers mapped addresses from 1 to 425 for address type VW, whereas I need only registers 8501 and 8502.

You're approaching this from the wrong perspective. If [product_name] acts as the server and, say, a Modbus PLC is the client, that PLC may not recognize operands like V, VB, VW, or VD from [product_name], making it unable to address the VM memory area directly. That's why VW0 matches HR1 from the Modbus PLC's viewpoint: VW2 = HR2, VW4 = HR3, and so forth. In your situation, the VFD should function as the server and [product_name] as the client. Accordingly, HR8501 from the VFD should be mapped to VW0 and HR8502 to VW2. Remember, [product_name] uses an offset of +1 for Modbus addresses.

This should help! When setting up the text display, the green and blue screens in the editor don't represent separate physical displays—they're just part of the same configuration. Both the onboard LCD and the external display can show messages up to 32 characters. In the message text properties (under FILE), you can select various character sets for different languages. For example, choose the Chinese character set to get 16 characters per line, versus the default 12. Adjust the ticker speed to 200ms as well. Make sure to enable your chosen character set at the top of the message text function block. Keep in mind that special characters (like degrees or umlauts) take up 2 spaces. For extra long messages, type up to 32 characters, spanning both green and blue sections. There are two ways to display long messages: set the ticker to 'line by line' or 'character by character' and tick the corresponding line number. To show the message on the LCD, set the destination to display, or pick the external text display, or both. When you activate the function block, the long message will be shown on either display, toggling or scrolling according to your settings. You can create multiple messages by enabling a second character set, which can be switched with a flag. All of this is using just one out of many message texts, so there's plenty of flexibility. Try experimenting with these features!

Regarding question 1: Any block or constant with an output port must be terminated, whether it's digital or analog, except for flags and output blocks. Digital connections can be terminated by linking the output connector to another digital block or constant, flag, output block, or an open terminal. Analog outputs connect similarly—either to another analog block, flag, or output block. For question 2: VB is a byte (8 bits) in the VM area, with VB0 containing bits V0.0 to V0.7. IB is a byte (8 bits) from the input range; IB0 covers I1 to I8. For question 3: The local address is the device being set up; the remote address is the device it's connecting to. For question 4: The VM area is a data memory section used for communication with other devices. For example, setting a bit in the VM area (like V0.0) with a button in the app lets you use that address as a network address in your [product_name] program. For question 5: I'm unclear on the question.

I'm still slightly confused, but things are clearer. For example: 1. If I link I1 to X4, how is it reflected in the VM area? Is it V0.1 or V0.4, and why? 2. Is VM a shared memory for all bits coming from X (open connector)? 3. By 'open terminal' do you mean 'open connector'? 4. Is it only when connecting a digital input to an X connector that the bit can be mapped to VM? 5. Does VB refer to a byte from digital inputs and VW from analog? Are these stored as V0.0 in VM? 6. If sending one digital input bit as VB1.0, does it become V1.0 in VM? 7. What happens in VM if I send a signal from I3 to X1? 8. You mentioned IB0 includes inputs 1-7: If I press I1, does that mean IB 0.0, requiring a connection to X1 for V0.0, or can I link I1 to X3 for V0.2? 9. Is X essentially for transmitting bits to VM?

The X constant only terminates open outputs of digital blocks and is not related to the VM memory. The term 'open connector' is defined by [company_name]. To share an input state with another device, you use the VM area, not the X constant. State transfer can be done with an input byte (IB) or network output instead of X. In this hardware version, network outputs only send to a client device. For example, sending IB0 transmits the status of inputs I1 to I8 together. VB is a byte in VM, usable for both digital and analog data. Typically, VW (a 16-bit word) transfers numerical values, but it can also send digital info. I did not claim IB0 or VB0 contain I1 to I7; there is only IB0, IB1, and IB2: IB0 = I1 to I8, IB1 = I9 to I16, IB2 = I17 to I24.

Hello everyone, I am using a [product_name] for controlling industrial lighting. For security reasons, I need the lights to turn on automatically if the power supply is interrupted, meaning the output relays should remain closed during a power loss. Is there a [version_no] or model that has outputs (relay or digital) that are normally closed when the power fails? I could not find such a version so far. Is there any model that provides normally closed relay outputs? Thank you for your support. [user_name]

No, such a version does not exist for [product_name]. All relay variants only have one contact (normally open). Switching is possible only with relays that include a changeover contact, which provides both NC (normally closed) and NO (normally open) contacts.

For your scenario, you'll need to create a power circuit using contactors and similar hardware. It’s necessary to design your circuit with the awareness that your [product_name] only has NO outputs. I typically use external relays connected to [product_name] outputs, since external relays are more cost-effective to replace than the controller itself. With external relays, you can choose between NO and NC, depending on your needs. Be cautious! Your power circuit should prevent all lights from turning on simultaneously. Consider this in your design.

Thanks for the response. I’ll opt for digital outputs and use external relays so I can customize the behavior. By the way, I don’t understand why it's important that all lights do not switch on simultaneously. Isn’t that what happens when the controller loses power?

The initial switching current is always higher than the running current. If all lights turn on at once, the power supply might experience excessive current and shut off for safety. The final result depends on the types of switching equipment, lighting, cabling, and other factors. In large facilities, switching is often sequenced using multiple contactors to distribute peak current and avoid overloads. Phase balancing is also taken into account by design. (smile) Ultimately, your design might differ—my advice is simply to be careful.

Hello, How does [product_name] execute its program? How can we determine the sequence in which instruction blocks are processed?

[product_name] starts with Block 001, then Block 002, and continues in order. Can you share why you are interested in this? Personally, I just need a reliably functioning [product_name].

No specific reason—I'm simply curious. The block numbers seem to get rearranged when you modify sections of the program, but apparently this doesn't impact execution.

There isn't an official description of how [product_name] handles block execution, but based on my observations and tests, here are some patterns: 1. Blocks are reviewed from lowest to highest repeatedly until all complete. 2. A block won't run if its input-linked blocks haven't yet run, and each block only executes once per cycle. 3. Parameters update instantly when a block executes, but this doesn't change execution order. When you use parameters, you might notice things don't execute in your expected sequence.

[product_name] operates similarly to larger PLCs. Step 1: Copies input states to the input register. Step 2: Runs the program using the input register values. Changes in input status during the cycle won't affect the program until the next cycle. While running the program, changing parameters update immediately (for instance, counter states, outputs, etc.). The program executes blocks from 001 onwards, but this isn’t documented and might not always be true. Step 3: Copies output statuses to the outputs. Step 4: Restarts from step 1. So, a change in physical input (or output) during the cycle only impacts the program in the following cycle. This explains the programming warning: 'Recursions of Input of xxxblock can only connect to output by a Marker or Output.'

[user_name], we seem to agree. When I mention block input from another block, I mean a link from one block’s output to another block’s input connection—not an input from the register. My rules fit well with your step 2. Here's an example using three blocks (numbered accordingly): - Block 001: Mathematical Instruction, V1 = 5 * Set OUTPUT: When En="0", output is Last Value. Otherwise, it won’t function correctly. - Block 002: AND(EDGE) (Simulates one program cycle) - Block 003: Mathematical Instruction, V2 = 10 * Set OUTPUT: When En="0", output is Last Value. Connections: - Input I1 links to Block 002's first input - EN input of Block 001 connects to Block 002's output - EN input of Block 003 connects to Block 002's output - Block 003's P1 parameter links to Block 001's Aq parameter - Block 001 output goes to AM1 - Block 003 output goes to AM2 Testing: 1. Reset all blocks to zero in the simulator. 2. Turn Input 1 on/off. AM1 reads 5, AM2 reads 10. Block 003: P1 = 5, P2 = 10, Aq = 10. Execution explanation: - Block 001 is reviewed first but waits as 002 hasn't executed. - Block 002 executes (linked only to input registers); its output goes HIGH. - Block 003 executes since 002 already did; Aq on Block 001 is still zero, so Block 003 adds 0 + 10 for 10. - Now, all blocks are executed, the cycle ends. Test another setup: - Create Block 004 (AND(EDGE)), remove Block 002 - Link I1 to Block 004's input - EN of Blocks 001 and 003 connect to Block 004's output Run the same test: AM1 reads 5, AM2 reads 15. Block 003: P1 = 5, P2 = 10, Aq = 15. Blocks 002 and 003 were skipped initially (since 004 hadn't executed). Block 004 ran after 003 was checked. On the second round, 002 and 003 executed because 004 was already done. This logic lets you predict block behavior. [product_name] might use a more advanced system internally, but this matches observable behavior.

First, make sure your [product_name] is powered by DC (12V or 24V). Second, use a 500-ohm resistor: 20mA x 500 ohm equals 10V, so 0-20mA x 500 ohm gives 0-10V, and 4-20mA x 500 ohm gives 2-10V. Third, connect the positive DC supply to your sensor, sensor output to both the resistor and the [product_name] analog input (I7 or I8), then connect the other side of the resistor to the negative DC supply. For programming, assign I7 as Ai1 or I8 as Ai2.

For the [product_name] Basis, only certain [article_no] versions are supported. For [product_name] Pure, there are other specific [article_no] versions. With the newer version ([article_no]), additional input options like I1 can be used as Ai3, and I2 as Ai4.

Hello everyone in this discussion. Here are some possible reasons: 1) If the sensor has 4 wires, 2 are for power and the other 2 are for the 0/4..20mA output. You should connect a 500-ohm resistor across these 2 output wires, with the negative lead going to the [product_name] common and the positive to the analog input (I7, I8 for some [version_no] modules, and possibly I1 & I2 for newer ones). 2) If it's a 2-wire sensor, it must be loop-powered—connect the 24V DC supply to the positive lead, the negative lead to the [product_name] analog input, and put the resistor between the common and negative signal line. 3) Many sensors don't work well with more than 250 ohm resistance in the loop. In that case, use a 250-ohm resistor and adjust scaling in the [product_name] program. 4) It's better to use precision resistors with low tolerance rather than standard ones because inaccurate resistance values can affect scaling and signal stability, especially due to temperature changes. I hope this clarifies things for everyone.

Hello everyone, I'm having trouble with [product_name] and [product_name]. I'm confused why the marker AM15 and the output for B004 is 34, which is correct, but the output for NAQ1 (memory VW4) is only 3. Thank you for your help!

Your problem is related to overlapping in the VM memory area. VW4 contains VB4 and VB5. VW5 contains VB5 and VB6. To avoid overlap, use NAQ2 with VW6.

Can you elaborate more on this overlapping issue? Thanks!

VM memory addressing is organized by bytes. The smallest unit is a bit; 8 bits make up a byte. Two consecutive bytes (16 bits) make a word, and two consecutive words (4 bytes or 32 bits) form a double word. For example, V0.0 refers to bit 0 in byte 0. VB0 contains bits V0.0 to V0.7. VW0 includes VB0 and VB1 (bits V0.0 to V1.7), and VD0 includes VW0 and VW2 (VB0 to VB3 or V0.0 to V3.7). In bit addresses, the number before the dot is the byte address; the number after is the bit within that byte. For word and double word addresses, the number indicates where the sequence starts. To prevent overlap when working with words, always use even addresses (VW0, VW2, VW4, etc.), and for double words, use multiples of four (VW0, VW4, VW8, etc.).

Is it possible to connect a 4-20 mA signal directly to the analog input of [product_name]? Or does the signal need to be converted to 0-10 Volt first?

Hello, These hidden function blocks often show up when you copy and paste in ladder diagrams. There isn't a direct link between FB and SF numbers since in [product_name], the FB numbers are generated automatically as you add blocks. SF flags are internal requirements in ladder logic and begin at 1. I recommend using function block diagrams instead of ladder diagrams.

What is the purpose of the FE (functional earth) terminal? I notice many [product_name] modules work fine without it, but it must have some function.

These clamps are meant for connecting the shielding of shielded cables, but one of these terminals should be attached to the PE. However, this should not be confused with a potential equalization terminal.

If I have only one [product_name] module, does that mean there's just a single FE terminal and I simply wire it to ground? From what I understand, it's standard to connect the shield of a shielded cable to PE, so what is the specific purpose of FE?

The idea is to keep the signal-carrying wire and its shield together for as long as possible before connection. If you separate them a meter before the connection point, the wire is exposed for that distance, which increases its susceptibility to interference.

I agree with your approach: carry the signal right to its endpoint and then connect it (say, after 60 meters) to PE instead of FE. Is there a difference between connecting to PE versus FE? There must be, but it's not clear to me.

The FE terminal on the [product_name] PLC module is primarily used for the network connection side. Under normal circumstances, the [product_name] PLC doesn't require it. It's generally intended for cases when non-shielded cables are used or the RJ45 connector lacks a shield. As [user_name] mentioned, the network relies on ground as a reference. I've also seen many installations without the FE terminal, using basic cables, which sometimes resulted in communication glitches. Adding a ground wire to the FE terminal resolved these issues. In my home setup, seven [product_name] PLC modules are on the same network as computers and other devices. I haven't yet connected the FE terminal to ground and have had no issues, but I use high-quality Cat6 cables with all shields grounded at the switches, except for short patch cables which are unshielded.

Thank you both for your explanations.

Everything appears correct. The value seen in the program simulation is not the output after the analog amplifier of the threshold block, but rather units from the analog input’s A/D converter. No matter if the analog signal is 0-10V, 0-20mA, or 4-20mA, it’s converted into 1000 units. For 4-20mA, the first 200 units represent the baseline, meaning the first 4mA equals zero. For your threshold block settings: Min = -100, Max = 400, Gain = 0.5, Offset = -100. If your input shows 438 units (about 8.76mA): 438 x 0.5 = 219, 219 - 100 = 119. So, the trigger won’t activate yet—only at 440 units (about 8.8mA) or more.

Additionally, your parameters don't align with the specified measuring range (-100 to 400 bar using 4-20 mA). With this range, your setup fits a 0-20 mA sensor better.

What’s the maximum value you need for meters per minute? For instance, if 32,767 m/min is sufficient, it’s best to calculate directly in mm/min and use three decimal places for accuracy. Regards, [user_name]

Hello, the speed is much lower than 32,768—maximum is around 10 m/min. So, is my speed calculation correct?

Your calculation seems fine, but 2 * Pi * 40 / 2000 * 1000 is about 125.66. To improve accuracy, you can change your formula: instead of multiplying by 60, multiply by 6; instead of dividing by 1000, divide by 10,000. Then, multiply by 12,566. So: mm/min = frequency * 6 * 12,566 / 10,000. Alternatively, adjust the gate time setting of the digital threshold trigger. One rotation equals 2 * Pi * 40 = 251.33 mm, or 2000 pulses, so each pulse is 0.1257 mm. For 10,000 mm/min, that’s 79,577 pulses/min, or about 1.33 pulses/s. For 1000 pulses, the cycle time is roughly 0.75s. If you set the gate time to 0.75s, calculations complete in one step. You just need arithmetic for decimal places, as the threshold trigger doesn’t allow decimal place settings. Your current method is valid, but this is another option. Regards, [user_name]

Thanks a lot for your suggestion about the alternative approach. I have another question: In B002 (the counter for actual distance), once it reaches 32,768 pulses, B007 can’t calculate further. If the total distance is 350 meters, how can I calculate and show this on the [product_name] display? Best regards, [user_name]

Split your counting into two stages: one counter for mm and a second for meters. For every 1000 mm, you get about 7,958 pulses. When the first counter hits 7,958, reset it and increment the meter counter by one. Display them as: mm = first counter * 1000 / 7958 and m = second counter directly. If cascading the counters is tricky or you need more details, feel free to ask. Regards, [user_name]

Hello, Relay failures here aren't necessarily due to poor quality. LED and energy-saving lamps on 230V AC are capacitive loads. When switching these, the inrush current can be over 100 times greater than the normal operating current. Such high inrush current can damage relay contacts. Components designed to limit the inrush current are recommended for these types of lamps. I hope this clarifies the situation.

The [product_name] detects communication errors in different ways, and sometimes does not recognize them at all. 1) If the client is switched to STOP mode, the server detects it and all memory bits (VB0 to VB850) are set low. 2) If the client loses power, the server does not notice and the bits keep their current state. 3) If the Ethernet cable is unplugged: 3.1) With direct connection, the server is aware but memory bits retain their state. You can detect this with a network input using the 'Ethernet error' diagnostic. 3.2) If connected via router, the server won’t recognize the disconnection and bits will not reset. Use a life bit query programmed in both units for better error handling.

The client generates a signal that changes state every second, sends it to the server, which checks if it's been HIGH or LOW for more than 1.5 seconds to detect communication loss. 's configuration seems unusual in this aspect. I'll think about possible workarounds.

I've found a neat solution to this problem. Please refer to the attached animated GIF. In this setup, the memory and output blocks update only at the end of each program scan, not instantly as the diagram might suggest. Therefore, changes are visible in the subsequent scan, effectively adding a one-scan delay for both activation and deactivation. By inserting a memory block between the output of the first shift register and the input of the next, bit 2.1 will activate just as bit 1.8 deactivates. Using this approach, it's possible to cascade all four shift register blocks (maximum allowed on [product_name] V8.3) to successfully create a 32-bit shift register.

I'm seeking advice on how to properly calibrate a pressure transducer. Everything is set up and working as expected so far. I connected my calibrated Druck DPI705 to the same source and noticed a 30 unit difference between the readings. Should I adjust the gain or the offset on the analog amplifier? Any help would be appreciated since this is my first time working with pressure transducers. I'd like to do it correctly before making any changes. The transducer is a 2.5 bar Absolute 4-20mA model used for vacuum control.

Try using two analog amplifiers in series for your setup.

Thanks for your suggestion, but I'm unsure how the settings on the pre-amplifier will account for the 30 unit difference, or any adjustment at all. Could you provide more details on how it works?

The analog input's A/D converter in a [product_name] module normally converts signals (such as 0-10V, 0/4-20mA, or PT100/1000) into a range of 0-1000 units. These units are then scaled with an analog amplifier to match the encoder's measuring range. For a 4-20mA sensor, the first 200 units represent the 4mA baseline, leaving 800 units for scaling. For example: from -1,000 to 1,500 bar is a span of 2,500 bar. So 2,500 / 800 = 3.125 for the gain factor. However, only two decimal places are supported for the gain, so rounding occurs (3.125 becomes 3.13), which introduces minor deviations in minimum, maximum, and offset. To address this, using two analog amplifiers in series helps. The first converts 800 units to 1000, and the second uses a gain factor (e.g., 2.5). The offset is then corrected so that the values align to the desired range, such as shifting 0.000 to 2.500 bar to -1.000 to 1.500 bar.

This thread was split from a discussion on connecting an input analog sensor (4-20mA) to a [product_name].

I want to connect sensors to all available analog inputs. My sensors output 4-20mA, and I plan to connect them to the base module using a 500 ohm resistor. However, I’m unsure about proper wiring setup.

Does your sensor have its own power supply, or is it just a 2-wire sensor?

No, the sensor lacks a dedicated power supply. It’s a 2-wire vibration sensor.

In this case, connect +24V from the [product_name]'s power supply to the sensor’s positive terminal. Connect the sensor’s negative terminal to one end of the resistor and to the analog input terminal of the [product_name]. Attach the other end of the resistor to the negative terminal (M) of the power supply.

Alternatively, you could use a 4-20mA to 0-10V signal converter. These are cost-effective and let you fine-tune zero and span settings for optimal input adaptation.

A 500 ohm resistor works well too. Any tolerance issues can be offset by using an analog amplifier.

Using a resistor results in a 20% loss in possible resolution, which can lead to missing values—so it's not always 'just as well.' This might be fine for some users. For example: - A dedicated 4-20mA to 0-10V converter gives you 1000 distinct values as output. - With a 500 ohm resistor (which I personally use and can confirm works), remember that: • Your sensor’s zero point is at 2V (200 units) • The max sensor value is at 10V (1000 units)

If someone is highly focused on achieving 100% resolution, they usually aren’t using a [product_name].

You're right about loss of resolution—optimal results require a suitable signal converter with offset and gain adjustment. However, most users connect analog signals directly to the base module to save money, avoiding an analog expansion module or converter. Consider both the accuracy of the analog inputs and the converter itself. Users often search for very precise resistors, but a 499 ohm resistor with 1% tolerance serves the same purpose and is inexpensive. You can calculate resolution as follows: - For 0..10V or 0..20mA, it's range/1000 - For 2..10V or 4..20mA, it's range/800 Then, determine what works best for your setup. Sometimes issues arise from using the wrong sensor, such as choosing one meant for 4000mm when you only need 2000mm, or opting for a sensor output of 4..20mA when other outputs might be more appropriate. Regards, [user_name]

Personally, I’m not a fan of [company_name] examples and I prefer to avoid drag-and-drop network connections. I always use manual mapping for better throughput. On your referenced site, you’ll see HR130 mapped to VW12, which means two registers (HR130 and HR131) are mapped to VW12 and VW14 (or VB12, VB13, VB14 and VB15—equivalent). For the F/I converter, the parameter VM12 is used. Selecting Float means two registers = two words = four bytes (next free address is VM16). Selecting Double uses four registers = four words = eight bytes (next free is VM20), but you need to handle four registers. If you have more sequential registers, you can transfer them in bulk—just select the correct number. Watch out for numbering: registers HR1, HR2, HR13 may be mapped to VW10, VW12, VW14, since the [product_name] variables are byte-oriented. There’s a limit on the number of registers you can transfer at once, perhaps around 125 registers. Regards, [user_name] P.S. If you want to read a single register (integer from -32768 to +32767), use an analog network input and select an appropriate VW number created in your client/server connection.

The issue is with the green blocks—these directly define the Modbus connection in the block itself. Use local mapping to VM memory instead; then you can organize the memory into areas for digital and analog signals. For sequences of eight digital signals with DI or coil, a compact design (see attachment) is better. For analog signals (holding registers in sequence), use another compact arrangement even if some values aren’t needed. Registers are 16 bit (one word, two bytes), so start VWx at an even number to avoid future issues. For floats (two registers, four bytes), begin VWx at a number divisible by four. For double (four registers, eight bytes), likewise. First, list all needed signals, then plan the VM memory to prevent overlaps and problems. Regards, [user_name]

The VM area ranges up to 851 bytes, from VB0 to VB850, freely available for user-defined purposes. For example: Bit addresses map as V0.0 = DB1.DBX0.0, V0.1 = DB1.DBX0.1, and so forth up to V850.7 = DB1.DBX850.7. Byte mappings: VB0 = DB1.DBB0, VB1 = DB1.DBB1, etc. Word: VW0 = DB1.DBW0 up to VW849 = DB1.DBW849. Double Word: VD0 = DB1.DBD0 up to VD847 = DB1.DBD847.

The [article_no] manual states that this device can only save up to 2000 records per datalog file on the SD card. Why is there such a limitation? I would expect an 8GB SD card to store much more data.

You are correct; the maximum number of datalog entries per file is 2000 for this hardware, and this cannot be modified. However, if you perform a RUN/STOP cycle, a new datalog file will be generated on the SD card. Using the software, only the most recent datalog file can be accessed; to read older files, you need to use a card reader. The remaining space on the SD card can still be used for other data, such as documentation or service packs.

Although the restriction may seem problematic, it is sufficient in most real-world cases. There are alternative approaches available, and ultimately, it’s important to evaluate how these data management options align with your project needs.

The maximum number of entries is set at 2000, and this cannot be changed. Regards, [url]

Hello everyone, I'm creating a control program for the shutters in my home. Everything generally works as intended (timed closing, alarm integration, etc.), but I need assistance displaying the shutter position. For example, in my test setup (see attachment), the values on outputs may eventually exceed 28 or drop below 0. Could someone guide me on how to address this issue? Thank you in advance for your quick response. Best regards, [user_name]

This issue is expected since you're using two timers without physical limit switches, and operate outputs for preset durations. For instance: if your system restarts, both timers are at zero. When you command the shutter to move up, then stop by briefly activating the opposite direction, the timer for the movement direction might stop at 15 seconds. If you next activate the down direction and let it run uninterrupted, the timer counts 28 seconds. When calculating position, you subtract the 'up' value from the 'down' value: 15s - 28s = -13s. Without a sensor counting actual movement, these offsets will always occur.

Thank you for your reply. I understand this issue. My question is whether it's possible to determine the shutter's position, using only open/close timings, without encoders. Perhaps another function block might help, or maybe restricting the counter range to between 0 and 28 could solve it? It's a basic shutter—the total movement time is 28 seconds up or down. If you apply longer running time, limit switches will stop the motor. Open to any suggestions :-) Best regards, [user_name]

Is that even feasible? Without an encoder, you cannot reliably know the shutter's position—there's no way to account for all partial movements. If you change direction mid-way, the full movement time isn't always used. Without synchronization, these offsets remain.

Try checking the program attached. In that example, the movement is monitored with a pulse counter. Upward movement is capped when the counter reaches 28 (seconds) and downward movement can never go below zero, preventing negative values entirely.

Hello [user_name], This type of problem is often encountered: counting pulses over a time interval and converting the result to a physical value. I previously shared solutions on the German forum. Here's a summary: One way is to use the "threshold trigger" function connected to an input pin. If you set the time interval (gate time) parameter, you get the input signal's frequency. You can adjust the gate time to convert pulses into desired units, for example, by applying a translation factor. However, the manual specifies limitations on the minimum gate time, and you can only display the value, not use it further within other [product_name] functions. Another option is to add a frequency divider before the threshold trigger. Using blocks like counter and digital flag, you can set parameters so the trigger function receives the input frequency divided by a factor. This allows you to adjust the gate time and scaling accordingly, but again, you can only display the value. To overcome these restrictions, I programmed a modified threshold trigger. Check the attached example (comments are in German). In summary: replace certain simulation blocks with an input signal, set an impulse generator to define the gate time, and use a counter to count pulses within each measurement interval. The result is held in a memory block and then amplified to convert to the correct units, adjusting for decimals as needed. Advantages of this approach: 1) You can reference the scaled result in other logical blocks, 2) You can adjust display precision, and 3) You can synchronize multiple triggers. Hope this explanation helps you solve your issue. Best regards [user_name]

Hello everyone! I attempted to measure feedback time using a Stopwatch function as shown in the attached example. Can someone assist me with integrating a comparator to check the time difference between each Stopwatch instance? If the difference between the two Stopwatch readings surpasses 50ms, I want it to indicate a failure. Thank you in advance.

You could use three analog comparators, correct?

No.

The Stopwatch’s measured value is 32 bits wide (DWord), but the analog comparator handles only 16-bit inputs. If the time value goes beyond 32,767, the Stopwatch keeps running, but the analog comparator stops at 32,767. So, using a simple analog comparison works only if the value stays below 32,767.

Your settings for the comparators are incorrect. The minimum time unit for the Stopwatch is 1/100s, not 1/1000s. If you click on the block, you’ll see 1/100s as the base value. Although the block is labeled as "ms", 1 unit is actually 10ms. Therefore, you need to enter 5, not 50, into the comparator; the circuit works only if the measured time doesn’t exceed 5 minutes, 27 seconds, and 67 hundredths. Now you have a foundation for your next step with CR6. I can't provide detailed help for that device, but can assist with Modbus in general. If you encounter Unit ID issues, adjust the relevant settings in your Modbus client software for [product_name]; default value is 255. Make sure the same Unit ID parameter is set on both CR6 and [product_name] to ensure proper communication (for example, use 1). The holding register numbers 1 and 5 in my test program are just examples—you can use any number, as long as those registers exist in CR6. If registers are consecutive, you can simplify client settings by just using the starting register and increasing the block length as needed (2, 3, 4...). Remember, Modbus registers are 16-bit, while [product_name] variables may be 8-bit. Reading 4 registers starting from VW10 leads to the next ones at VW12, VW14, and VW16. The word VW10 covers bytes VB10 and VB11, so the following available number would be 12. With 4 registers in VW10 to VW16, you shouldn't use bytes VB10 to VB17 or bits V10.0 to V17.7 to avoid overlapping memory values. Good luck with your project, [user_name]

The S0 interface transmits measured data using impulses. These impulses can have a frequency lower than 1Hz and a width of 30ms. Hello, my understanding is as follows: For frequency measurements, a 50% duty cycle is usually required. If the pulse duration is less than 50%, it changes the requirements. A 30ms pulse requires the input's ability to detect that short period. If the device is limited to 4Hz, it likely cannot detect a 30ms pulse reliably. Which [product_name] and [article_no] are you using? The DC versions offer built-in high-speed counters, with some supporting up to 5kHz depending on the model. Testing it may help clarify. The input frequency for DC versions depends on the device's cycle time, so review the manual (be sure to reference your specific [product_name] version and use the correct manual). For example, in [product_name] V8, the function block cycle is typically under 0.1ms. If you use around 400 function blocks, the total cycle time is about 40ms. So with programs under 300 function blocks, handling these pulses may work. The manual also describes how to measure cycle time. Hope this helps.

[user_name]: Unfortunately, [product_name] only provides 4 fast inputs, and its expansion modules do not provide additional fast inputs. [user_name]: My preferred model is the 12/24RCE(o). Regarding frequency definitions, if the specification lists 'frequency,' it likely refers to a 50% duty cycle signal. If a signal isn't 50/50, perhaps it doesn't technically have a 'frequency.' Possibly, [company_name] means the frequency for signals with a balanced duty cycle. For your point about 4Hz and a 30ms pulse: It depends on the internal implementation. If each input has an interrupt latch, in theory it should detect impulses down to 1 microsecond, provided they don't repeat more than once every 0.25 seconds. If inputs operate just as I/O leads, then impulses shorter than 0.25 seconds may not be detected. This specific behavior is not documented.

Hello, the minimum pulse length that a [product_name] can detect is critical for your application. This depends on input/output delays and device scan time. The manual provides examples for calculating scan time. For instance, if the scan time is 100ms, the shortest pulse detectable is approximately 101ms. That corresponds to 10Hz. If you have 10ms pulses with a period of 100ms (10Hz), the device will not capture these pulses. The scan process for a [product_name] is roughly: read inputs, run the user program, and write outputs. Note that unlike a PLC, [product_name] does not have input interrupts or pulse capture features. There may be alternative solutions, though. Can you provide more details about your application, such as frequency, minimum pulse length, and any other constraints regarding S0 pulse counting?

In summary, handling S0 pulses requires fast inputs. However, this leads to a new concern: can a fast input reliably detect every 30ms pulse, even if the scan cycle exceeds 100ms? If not, then the fast input of [product_name] may still be unable to process S0 interface signals accurately.

If you have a digital output, such as Q1, in a [product_name] module, you cannot change the output state through Modbus if it's being handled by the program. Hello, I need advice. I'm measuring temperature using four Pt100 sensors connected with two [product_name] modules. The [product_name] manual mentions a recommended cable length of 10 meters. Thanks in advance for any suggestions.

Hi [user_name], interesting question! One advantage of our PT100 module is that it supports 3-wire measurements. This setup lets the module estimate the resistance of the lead wires, which is useful for calculating the true temperature at the sensor tip. Unlike signal measurement with 0/4..20 mA, temperature is measured using the resistance of a platinum filament—100 ohms at 0.01 °C. Lead length, wire thickness, and local temperatures can affect resistance. Using 3 wires, the module corrects for lead resistance before relaying results to the [product_name] system. For 2-wire sensors, accuracy depends on wire quality and environment. The manual recommends 10 meters of shielded wire for best accuracy (as noted on page 263). With 15 meters, accuracy may decline by about 50%, e.g. from ±1.0% to ±1.5% for positive temperature ranges and even more in the negative range. A 3-wire setup greatly reduces this loss of accuracy. I hope this helps. You can find more information about temperature measurement principles online. (Background: experience in temperature and humidity calibration, standards, and measurement applications — always interesting to see these principles in use with [product_name].)

Hello, I found a solution for the [product_name] error: You can use a network analyzer tool (such as Microsoft Network Monitor 3.4, which is free) to identify what software is initiated when you access the [product_name] device. Look for Javaw.exe, along with the destination IP address and port number, to determine which software is using that IP. In my case, the problem was caused by pass-through from another software. In the Parameter-VM-Mapping table, use the parameters in DWord format. The addressing in [product_name] is byte-oriented. A DWord consists of 32 bits, or 4 Bytes, or 2 words. If you use address 2 for the first DWord, you are utilizing VB2 through VB5. If the second DWord uses address 3, it occupies VB3 through VB6, leading to overlap. Therefore, after using address 2 for the first DWord, the next logical address should be 6, not 3.

Could you clarify what you mean by 'online simulation mode'? In [product_name] programming software, there is a simulation mode and an online mode. The online mode shows current states and values from a connected [product_name]. Without seeing your program, it's difficult to determine why M1 flashes intermittently.

Having a 3-wire sensor does not guarantee direct compatibility with every input. Your sensor uses an NPN open collector output, which functions like a relay contact bridging the output to 0V. [product_name] inputs are PNP type and require a positive voltage to detect a high signal. Think of the open collector output as a relay contact connecting the input to 0V, essentially acting like an unconnected input. Combining the external resistor with the internal resistor (~72 kOhm) of the [product_name] input forms a voltage divider. For example, using a 10 kOhm resistor, when the output is open, 24V is split across both resistors, resulting in around 21V at the input—sufficient for a high signal. Reducing the resistor increases the voltage further, but isn't necessary for a high level. When the output is closed, the input drops to 0V and current through the open collector is 24V / 10kOhm = 2.4 mA; ensure it doesn't exceed 10 mA. For exact voltage levels, consult the operating instructions for your [product_name] and sensor documentation.

Could someone explain how to handle this value at VW2? The manual outlines these common steps for converting float/integer: 1) Transfer float data via Modbus to VM. 2) Convert float data in VM to integer using a converter. 3) Work with the converted integer. 4) Convert back to float if needed. Are these the correct steps I should follow? If possible, could you provide a simple example? I would appreciate it very much. Thanks.

The addressing in [product_name]'s VM memory is byte-oriented. To input a 32-bit float, you need to use 4 bytes—transfer VB0 to VB3 (VW0 + VW2). For conversion, use the F/I converter at VM0. To reverse it (integer to float), use an I/F converter—enter VM4 so it covers VB4 to VB7 (VW4 + VW6). These 4 bytes must then be sent to two Modbus registers.

Hi [user_name], thank you for your reply! I am already using VM=0 with the float/integer converter, as shown in my code, but it's not working. I’m unsure about your point on 'inputting a 32-bit float via VB0 to VB3 (VW0 + VW2)'. If I send data from HR=11 to VW0 (long=2), shouldn’t the data be available at VB3? In the data table, I see bits marked V3.0 to VB3.7, but only receive float values up to 255. I've attached my [product_name] code.

To clarify: VM memory is addressed by byte, while Modbus holding registers are addressed by word. A 32-bit Modbus value consists of 4 bytes (2 words), using two consecutive registers, e.g. HR11 and HR12. Similarly, in [product_name]'s VM memory, it uses 4 bytes or 2 words. For transfer, only the start address for the VM region in [product_name] is set; a 32-bit value from HR11 gets written to VW0, and HR12 to VW2. The converted integer is shown on the output (Aq) of the F/I converter, not at the VM locations themselves. Additional notes: In [product_name], holding registers start at address 1; if Arduino starts at 0, add an offset of 1 to the connection table. That means Arduino's register 11 is HR12 on [product_name] if Arduino starts at 0, and HR11 otherwise. I do not know if the Arduino Unit ID is 255, and you must make sure the F/I converter uses the correct resolution for your integer values.

You can experiment in simulation mode. Make a program using F/I (VD0), followed by an analog amplifier. Add a message display tied to the analog amplifier parameter. During simulation, add VD0 to the data table as a float format. Enter a test value like 1.2 in the 'new value' column. The resulting value will show in the message text. Adjust the F/I properties or the amplifier as needed. Note that [product_name] does not support floating-point calculations directly, so further processing must be done using integers. Hope this is helpful.

Also, how is the address of the first digital input on the second base module determined? Is it coded as I1 (similar to the first base module) or I25, or does it use a different scheme?

Hello, you do not lose any inputs. You can use network inputs for communication between the modules. The inputs on the second module are still referred to as I1. If you want to utilize them in the first module, you need to use network inputs.

A [product_name] [version_no] can support a maximum of 24 digital inputs, 20 digital outputs, 8 analog inputs, and 8 analog outputs. A basic module with 8 digital inputs and 4 digital outputs, plus two DM16 extension modules, reaches the maximum digital I/O capacity for a single basic module. Additional DM16 extension modules will not be recognized by a single basic module. Therefore, to achieve 72 inputs and 60 outputs, you need three basic modules networked together. Each basic module uses the same addressing convention: I1-I24 for inputs and Q1-Q20 for outputs, plus AI1-AI8 and AQ1-AQ8 for analog. To make inputs and outputs from one base module available in another, you must transfer them through the network using network inputs and outputs.

When [company_name] provides a Modbus driver, it tries to adhere to Modbus specifications (originally designed for Modicon PLCs) on its hardware. Modbus registers are 16-bit and mainly transmit word-sized values, typically integers in specific ranges. Floating-point (REAL) numbers require two sequential registers because they use 32 bits, formatted per IEEE 754. If volts start at address 2 in the mapping, read both address 2 and 3, and move them into a 32-bit REAL register in your [product_name] program to interpret the value. Typically, it's more important to select the correct offset than the function code (3 or 4), unless your mapping differs significantly. Here’s an IEEE 754 conversion example: If the value is 240.0 Volts, you’ll send the corresponding binary and hexadecimal 32-bit values through two Modbus registers. Hope this clarifies things. Edit: I saw your discussions with [user_name] and noticed [product_name] is involved in your setup. However, [product_name] CPUs can't process floating point numbers internally. Consider checking out an alternative in this [url] or upgrading to [version_no] PLC.

The setup involves RouterOS continuously reading modbus holding registers from the [product_name] every second. If a value exceeds a set limit, the [product_name] sets an 'alarm bit.' While RouterOS can calculate threshold exceedances, it's easier to do this within the [product_name]. Boolean operations like setting or resetting bits are more challenging in RouterOS scripts but achievable with persistence using bit-shifting and masking.

However, the cycle time is undefined and usually does not match 50 ms or 300 ms, risking inaccurate filtering of analog signals. 2. If you're following my example, the value assigned to parameter V1 (from HMI) is multiplied by parameter V2 (which should be set to 2 or 20 based on your needs). Hello everyone! This is an important topic. It was discussed on the German forum under the link [url]. This color change error in [product_name] version [version_no] happens if: - You close the software while simulation is running - The software or Windows crashes during simulation - You save the program while simulation is running - You simulate more than one program at once and any of the above happens The issue is that the software saves the line color settings with the program itself. The steps below are a bit lengthy but solve the issue. I've translated them here—feel free to print them out for reference! 1) Open your affected program 2) Zoom out until you see the entire program 3) Go to TOOL --> OPTIONS --> COLOURS, select BLACK for simulation colors and APPLY/OK 4) Make a small change in the program (add and delete a block or move one slightly) 5) Start SIMULATION mode and check all lines are black 6) While simulation is running, close the software 7) When asked to save because of changes, select YES and save (either same or new file) 8) Reopen the software—make sure it's the only open instance! 9) Open your newly saved program 10) Return to TOOLS --> OPTIONS --> COLOURS and set the standard colors for everything, then APPLY/OK 11) Repeat this for every affected program, since the error is saved in each one—not just a global setting Hope this helps! A key lesson: Always stop simulation and return to editing mode (ensuring lines turn black) before saving or making any changes. Also, only run one simulation at a time. This is good programming practice. Good luck managing the color changes!

Hello everyone, I have two questions about the special flag M8 (power reset): 1) What is the relationship between the power reset and the retentive flag for special functions? For instance, if I set the R parameter for a latching relay and connect the R (reset) pin to M8 (power reset), what will happen? Does the power reset clear the latching relay and then restore its state from before the power failure, or does it overwrite the retained state? 2) Is it possible to access M8 (power reset) from within a user-defined function (UDF)? Sometimes it's necessary to reset a pulse relay at startup, but if the relay is inside a UDF, direct access to M8 seems unavailable. I appreciate any advice.

The special flag M8 serves as a startup indicator. After a device restarts, M8 goes high only during the initial cycle, which is useful for triggering specific actions right after startup.

However, the core question remains: Is this executed before or after the retention process? If it's after, will it overwrite the retained state?

Please refer to the attached document for further details.

If you use an RS relay with retention enabled, and the relay is ON when the device loses power, after power is restored, the RS relay will also be ON. But if you connect the R input to the M8 flag, the RS relay will be OFF during the first cycle after power-up and will stay OFF until you set it again. When powering up any programmable logic device, the initial step sets all retentive values (timers, counters, relays, etc.) to those stored before power loss. The program then proceeds with the first cycle: 1. Read all input statuses and store in registers 2. Execute the program, writing outputs to registers 3. Update outputs with the values in the registers 4. Repeat from step 1 Throughout one cycle, the input status remains consistent. Any input change during step 2 will be processed in the following cycle. If you want M8 used in both the main program and in a UDF, you need to first utilize M8 in the main program and connect it as an input to your UDF.

Thanks everyone! 1) If I understand correctly, the retentive function executes before any part of the program. This means the elements' states are first restored, and then the circuit behavior, such as power reset via M8, begins. 2) Unfortunately, my user-defined function doesn't have enough I/O pins to accommodate M8 as an input.

Hi [user_name], thanks for the [product_name] example. What calculations are needed to modify the output ranges?

This setup uses a simple linear equation for each segment. The general formula is: Input value * Gain + Offset Example: Input range: 3.01V to 5.00V Output range: 2.50V to 4.50V Given Input value: 4.00V Gain calculation: (Output Max - Output Min) / (Input Max - Input Min) Gain = (450 - 250) / (500 - 301) = 1.005 Offset calculation: Output Min - Input Min * Gain Offset = 250 - 301 * 1.005 = -53 Output value: Input value * Gain + Offset = 400 * 1.005 - 53 = 349 (which is 3.49V)

There are two general methods for calculating the arithmetic average. The first is to store all values, sum them, and divide by the count. There’s also a second method, usable in S7: accumulate values directly and track a counter. This method doesn’t work in [product_name] due to 16-bit integer limits (-32768 to +32767). Also, check if arithmetic average is the correct calculation type for your needs—Wikipedia lists arithmetic, geometric, harmonic averages... Best regards, [user_name]

Your PC and [product_name] device are on different subnets with different subnet masks and gateways. The device is on subnet 192.168.0.x, while the PC is on 169.254.142.x, so they can't communicate. The first three numbers in the IP should match on both, but the fourth should differ. Both subnet masks must also match, e.g., 255.255.255.0. If a gateway is used and devices connect via a router, it must be the same for both devices.

Assign your PC an IP address manually, such as 192.168.0.120, ensuring the same subnet and gateway as [product_name]. The 169.x IP address appears because you're not connected to a DHCP server to assign an IP. According to RFC5735, the 169.254.0.0/16 range is allocated for link-local communication, auto-assigned when DHCP is unavailable.

Hello everyone, I'm working on a network project that includes four [product_name] units with [version_no] and a HMI panel. I'm new to connecting HMI to [product_name], and I suspect there are some issues with address configuration in my program. When running online, certain network inputs unexpectedly switch states without any indication on the screen, appearing to respond to analog input values in the code. I suspect there may be address conflicts. Is there a recommended approach or guideline for structuring address allocation in such setups? I utilize digital and analog inputs/outputs, flags, network IOs, and VM mapping for parameter adjustments. For example, would assigning the same byte on different [product_name] units with distinct IP addresses cause issues? Since each [product_name] has a unique IP, does the HMI treat them separately? I found some forum lists showing standard VM addresses, would it be preferable to use those rather than assigning them myself? Any advice on network setup would be appreciated. Thanks!

Because I am not familiar with your [product_name] programs or HMI configuration, I can only make an educated guess. I suspect there is overlap in the VM storage region. Addressing within VM memory is based on bytes. For bits: address format is byte address, bit address, e.g., V0.0 means Byte0.Bit0. For bytes: a byte consists of 8 bits, for example, VB0 encompasses bits V0.0 - V0.7. For words: a word is made of two bytes, the starting address is the left byte, VW0 covers VB0 and VB1, or V0.0 - V1.7. For dwords: a dword has four bytes, with the left byte as the start address, VD0 covers VW0 and VW2, or VB0 - VB3, or V0.0 - V3.7.

Hello [user_name], thank you for your response! I found your addressing scheme on the forum—it clarified things and I've already tried it. Can I use V0.0 on [product_name] 1 (with IP 192.168.1.10) and reuse V0.0 on [product_name] 2 (IP 192.168.1.20)? Is there any conflict in the HMI, or does each IP keep things separate? To prevent issues, I've reorganized all VM and network input parameters, and will test tomorrow to see if the spontaneous switching is resolved.

Each [product_name] maintains its own memory space. You can transmit V0.0 from one [product_name] to the HMI without issue, so long as each [product_name] has a separate connection. The HMI uses the connection details to distinguish which V0.0 belongs to which [product_name].

Understood! I think I've identified my mistake. I started allocating addresses to network inputs before setting up VM mapping. [product_name] software automatically begins with VW0, and this overlapped with some of my NI addresses. I’ll be able to test and confirm this tomorrow. Thank you for your assistance!

That's the issue. If you assign V0.0 - V1.7 for digital bits, you cannot use VW0 elsewhere—doing so causes address overlap.

Because your PC is in a different subnet, [product_name] software creates a temporary IP for your PC to communicate with [product_name]. Once you quit the software or shut down the PC, the temporary IP disappears. To change [product_name]'s IP, create a small program (for example, I1 on Q1). Set the desired IP (192.168.1.33), with subnet mask 255.255.255.0, in the file properties, then transfer this to [product_name] using the temporary IP (192.168.0.254). During the transfer, the software will ask if the IP should be overwritten; confirm to change [product_name]'s IP to 192.168.1.33. For remote access, simply entering the port after the IP (like 192.168.1.33:8080) may not work if your router blocks the connection. Activate port forwarding on your router for port 8080 to 8080, but be cautious, as this exposes your device to security risks. Using DynDNS or VPN is safer for remote control.

Let me clarify some basics: The analog converter of [product_name] converts input signals into units ranging from 0-1000, regardless of whether it is 0-10V or 0/4-20mA. For a 4-20 mA signal, the initial 0-4 mA is outside the usable range, leaving you with 800 units (since 20 mA - 4 mA = 16mA). Here's the breakdown: 0 mA = 0 units, 4 mA = 200 units, 6 mA = 300 units, ... up to 20 mA = 1000 units. To set up the analog amplifier, you would use: Gain: 1.25 for a total of 1250 units. Offset: -250 so 1250 -250 = 1000 units. Min: 0 (offset correction), Max: 1000 (offset correction included). For example, at 6 mA the number after A/D conversion is 300. 300 * 1.25 (Gain) = 375, then 375 - 250 (Offset) = 125. The final, processed value is 125, which at one decimal is 12.5.

Hello all! Yes, the [product_name] 12/24RC(o), 24RC(o) and 230RC(o) models include potential-free relay outputs. The internal program only closes the relay contacts. Hello everyone, I recently started working with PLC programming and am currently using this PLC device. Programming is going well, but now I need to share some data from my analog inputs with our company's SCADA system. For example, I have a PT1000 sensor on AI1 linked to an analog threshold trigger [article_no], and its output is mapped in my software as a Word at address VW4. The SCADA communicates using S7 drivers, and I've already configured the server connection on the [product_name] device including the correct TSAP, which works for reading digital input bits. However, I'm unable to read the value from VW4, which I've mapped. What physical address should I use in the SCADA tag to access VM mapped values like in my setup? Sorry if anything is unclear—I'm still new to this and appreciate any guidance. Thanks in advance for any help!

There aren't special SCADA addresses within the VM memory area. Any unused address in the VM memory space can be used. It's important to understand how the memory area is structured to prevent overlapping accesses. The user-accessible memory area is 851 bytes, from byte 0 to byte 850, and is addressed by byte. For bits: Vx.y, where x is the byte address and y the bit inside the byte (e.g., V0.0). For bytes: VBx, representing each byte (e.g., VB0 = V0.0 to V0.7). Word is VWx, composed of 2 bytes (e.g., VW0 = VB0 + VB1 = V0.0 to V0.7 plus V1.0 to V1.7). DWord is VDx, made of 2 words; VD0 = VW0 + VW2 = VB0 + VB1 + VB2 + VB3, covering bits V0.0 to V3.7.

Hello [user_name], I appreciate your answer. I had already read your helpful PDF attached to another forum topic! That's why I'm unsure why I can't see output on my SCADA. I'm attaching a section of my software with Q1, which I used to check the SCADA and [product_name] connection linked to SCADA via I/O physical address Q0.0. Based on your PDF and these tests, I expected the physical address for my [article_no] to be VW4, but it's not showing any value.

Everything in your program looks correct, and there's no overlapping. Are you aware that the value in VW4 is an integer value? What type of SCADA system are you using?

Just to clarify: Should I be able to view any Word value I've mapped by inspecting it bit by bit? Specifically, if I look at bits V4.0 to V4.7 and V5.0 to V5.7, should I see boolean values that match my mapped Word?

In Parameter-VM-Mapping, 'Word' refers to the data width (16 bits), not the data type. Byte is 8 bits, Word is 16 bits, and DWord is 32 bits.

Good afternoon. Can someone explain how to organize a step-by-step program where each stage follows the previous one in sequence, in an efficient way? Currently, I am using delay blocks to control the steps.

Could you clarify your question? Are you referring to creating a sequencer?

I'm not a professional programmer, but I'll try to give an example. Suppose I need to switch on outputs Q1 and Q2 for ten minutes, then turn them off and switch on Q3 until AI1's value exceeds a certain threshold. Afterwards, Q1 and Q2 are turned on again for twenty minutes before the sequence finishes. The next stage only begins once the previous one is complete by time or event, and no other parts of the program run until the loop is done.

These questions are quite broad, and there are no one-size-fits-all solutions. Generally, there are two main ways to create a sequencer: - You can use latching relays to enable each step. After checking the necessary conditions, you move to the next step and reset the previous one. - Alternatively, you can use a shift register; the set bit triggers the corresponding action, and the bit moves forward when conditions are met. In both approaches, you can pause progression until a specific condition occurs.

The system consists of one PC, a central controller, and 11 remote controllers over 2.2 km. Given the distance, I was considering using several RS485 extenders (about every kilometer or less) and connecting everything using MODBUS. Is this feasible, and what challenges might arise? Thanks in advance.

Unless [product_name] is notably different from the standard, it utilizes Modbus TCP/IP (ethernet) instead of RTU. Using fiber optics might be your best choice; it would simplify the setup compared to employing extenders.

The [product_name] variant has Ethernet functionality equivalent to the standard version. However, to use Modbus TCP/IP, it must be an FS4 model ([version_no], second generation or newer). Previous generations, like the first [version_no], can only use Ethernet TCP/IP and not Modbus TCP/IP.

Sharing my experience: for devices requiring MODBUS RTU, I use affordable MODBUS TCP-to-RTU converters (e.g., Protoss PE11). It's essential to have a separate converter for each device, as polling multiple devices through one converter may cause communication issues—if a device does not respond, the subsequent addresses might not be polled. For instance, with devices at addresses 2, 3, 4, and 5 in the network, if address 3 fails to reply, devices 4 and 5 won't be polled since they appear as a single device with one IP address. So, using one converter per device solves this problem, and fortunately, these converters are not costly.

I am currently using a [product_name] device with [product_name] version [version_no]. The LCD is set up to show the circuit status—either DEPLOYING or DEPLOYED. According to my ladder diagram, there are Momentary and Limit switches that activate the motor coil when certain conditions are met. While the LCD correctly switches between 'LEFT DEPLOYING' and 'LEFT DEPLOYED' based on the circuit status, the displayed message depends on their priority settings. I'm wondering if there is a better way to control which message is shown, perhaps using conditional logic or another method. I'm new to ladder diagram programming and open to suggestions for improving my design.

When multiple messages are active at once, their priority decides which message gets shown. You can set the priority number when you create the message—0 is the lowest, and 127 is the highest.

I recommend using Function Block Diagram (FBD) instead of Ladder Diagram (LAD) for this application. LAD setups can be more complex and less intuitive, especially since the message block needs to be connected to an output, flag, or open connector, which isn't obvious in LAD. The FBD approach, as illustrated in the shared sample image, makes message block connections more apparent. It's fine to have several messages active at once, and navigating between them is possible using the up and down buttons. Keep in mind that any new message activation cancels navigation and displays the highest priority message. It's best to use lower priorities (under 100) for regular settings, and set higher priorities (above 100) for alarms or notifications. Try replicating the shared example, simulating switch actions to see how messages appear. Note that the sample image lacks open connector blocks; these are essential for loading configurations to the device but not required during simulation. Use the F2 key to check compile messages.

Hi, To explain, TSAP stands for Transport Service Access Point and historically comes from the time when controllers did not have built-in Ethernet. Connections required a communication processor (CP), which needed to know its place in the network configuration (now it's typically defined by rack and slot). When configuring communication between two [product_name] devices, each channel is assigned its own TSAP. [product_name] supports eight channels, so the first Ethernet connection uses TSAP 20.00, the second 21.00, and so forth. HMI panels are different; they require a TSAP of 02.00 on the controller side. If the correct TSAP isn’t used in a [product_name] to [product_name] exchange, the connection will not work.

Hi, I think there has been a misunderstanding. Regarding relay outputs: All [product_name] Base and DM8/16 modules use the same types of relays. Every relay output is potential-free, allowing different voltages for each relay. Maximum load varies: Base modules handle 10A, DM8 or DM16 modules only 5A. From the manual (page 292): Insulation strength meets IEC61131-2 requirements. To know the test voltage, you will need the details from the IEC standard. For 230V inputs: Single-phase power—All 230V versions and DM8/16 230V modules require inputs to be connected to the same phase as the device supplies. Example: If powered by L1, the inputs must use L1. For three-phase power: The Base Module has two input groups. Inputs I1 to I4 must use the same phase as the power (e.g., L1), while I5 to I8 can use either the same phase or another one (L2 or L3). Supplying the device with L1 and connecting L2 to I1-I4 will cause damage, but L2 at I5-I8 will not. DM8/16 modules: Same rule applies. DM8 powered by L1—the four inputs must use L1 only. For three-phase setups: Base module powered by L1 means inputs I1-I4 use L1 and I5-I8 can use L2 or L3. A third phase can be used for DM8 power supply and inputs. Product details and illustrations can be found in the manuals. Hope this clarifies things.

Hi [user_name]! For 0-10 V or 0/4-20 mA analog signals, you generally cannot measure them with two different devices (analog inputs) connected in parallel. The internal resistor networks within the devices convert current signals to voltage signals before analog-to-digital conversion, which can cause interference when connected in parallel. Instead, with your [product_name] controller, it makes sense to use the signal as an input, and then, via the program, branch that input directly to an output (or possibly through an analog amplifier with a gain of 1). By adding an analog output module, you can send the untouched signal to the second measuring device or analog input. This is my best suggestion — since you already have the [product_name] controller, it's more straightforward to add an analog output module than to seek a special signal splitter. This gives you a secondary output for other purposes, and you can handle all signal manipulation inside the [product_name] programming software, which is quite user-friendly.

Hello, I have a [article_no] [product_name] and I would like to control an analog clock that requires pulse inputs (one pulse per minute). Is it possible to create a pulse every minute, synchronized with the internal clock? I know I can use the asynchronous pulse function, but then the pulse isn't aligned with the device's clock (NTP). Is there a way to trigger a pulse when the seconds hit "00"? Thank you,

No, direct access to the internal time isn't available. You can only re-synchronize the asynchronous pulse generator with weekly timers at intervals you set.

As [user_name] pointed out, the time isn't accessible from within the [product_name]. Personally, I haven't tested whether the asynchronous pulse generator syncs with the clock—it's unlikely. You could try a workaround similar to how railway clocks work in Switzerland: use a slightly faster pulse than real time, then at the end of a defined period, wait for a precise trigger to start the next cycle. For example, you might use two weekly timers to send a pulse every 4 hours. During those 4 hours, an asynchronous pulse generator would emit a pulse every 59.99 seconds. After 3 hours, 59 minutes, and 57.6 seconds, the system sends its 240th pulse. It then waits for the weekly timer (synchronized via NTP to millisecond accuracy) to provide the next pulse and begins the next cycle in sync. Keep in mind, if the asynchronous pulse generator slows down unexpectedly, the system could become inaccurate—so you'll need to carefully test for consistency! Kind regards, [user_name]

[user_name], What is the switch connected to? If it's one of the [product_name] devices, the pulse stretching should be handled by the PLC itself. For example: input >> TOF (off-delay timer) >> network bit. In other control fields, we sometimes use a request-acknowledge approach: 1. Button >> set request memory bit 2. Request triggers networked bit 3. Partner PLC receives network bit 4. Partner PLC sends acknowledgement (memory bit + network bit) 5. Original PLC receives acknowledgement 6. Request memory bit + network bit are reset 7. Partner PLC receives reset 8. Partner PLC resets its own acknowledgement + network bit Hope this helps.

Hi, The issue is likely that data transfer takes longer than the duration of your button press. If you're using a master/master configuration, you can lengthen the pulse (using an off-delay) so it can be communicated to the other unit. In master/slave setups, only the master can do this, since the slave does not execute a program. Hope this helps.

It appears there’s been some confusion regarding your module type. You stated it was a 24RCE, but it’s actually the 12/24RCE version, which is significant. The 24RCE has no onboard analog inputs, while the 12/24RCE has four. By default, two are enabled (AI1 and AI2), and their addresses are reserved for the base module, regardless of usage. This means that the first analog channel on your RTD extension will be AI3. You should update the program address from AI1 to AI3 or disable the onboard analog inputs in your configuration.
