First, all details concern the device series [version_no]. 1) The [product_name] text display can communicate with only one logic module at a time. However, if multiple logic modules exist in a network, you can switch which one communicates with the display by changing its IP address in the display settings. Furthermore, one [version_no] module can connect with up to 16 others (8 static and 8 dynamic connections available).

When you mention 40-50Hz, do you mean engine speed or the frequency provided by a Variable Frequency Drive (VFD)? Standard asynchronous motors usually reach about 1500 RPM at 50Hz, which is quite fast. If your sensors' signals don't overlap, determining which comes first is even harder; keeping track of time delays between signals is critical. You’d need to measure the interval between i5 and i6, and vice versa, then compare these times to infer direction. This is complex even for larger PLCs. You might consider monitoring motor control commands (forward/reverse contactors with auxiliary contacts), or if using a VFD, connect its analog output to an analog input for feedback instead. These are just examples.

Hello, does anyone know what the maximum frequency of a digital transistor output can be? According to technical data, the transition from 0 to 1 and 1 to 0 takes around 1 ms for a transistor output, which suggests the maximum possible frequency is 500 Hz. Regards, [user_name]

Hello, the ON/OFF delay is just one factor. You also need to consider the scan time of the [product_name] device. Please refer to the manual for an example of calculating scan time. Typically, each function block adds around 0.1 ms to the scan time. If your program’s scan time is roughly 50 ms, you can determine the maximum achievable output frequency by considering: (ON delay + OFF delay + scan time)/1. About the register 406000: The following is general Modbus information, applicable to all Modbus implementations and not tied to any specific company or device. The leading digit '4' (e.g., 406000) designates a Holding Register, not an Input Register (Input Registers start with '3'). According to the Modbus specification, Input Registers are read-only, while Holding Registers are always readable and may be writable, depending on device firmware. Device documentation will state if the register is read-only or read-write. To read Holding Registers, use Modbus Function Code 03. To write to a single Holding Register, use Function Code 06. To write to multiple consecutive Holding Registers, use Function Code 16 (decimal) or 10 (hexadecimal). Assuming register 406000 is set up as read/write, this should be possible if permitted by the device.

Hello [user_name], This issue is more about contact load than the relay cycle time. Incorrect load on the contacts can cause relay failures.

Hi, It seems the problem relates to the type of load being switched. The description suggests the relay contacts are overheating and sticking together. Both valves and lamps present non-ohmic loads, which can affect relay lifespan. Valves might offer protection options from the vendor, but lamps are more difficult because they can create a substantial inrush current—sometimes thousands of times higher than normal—when switching on. To address this, an 'inrush current limiter' should be used in such scenarios; otherwise, the relays may fail shortly after installation. Coupling relays might only transfer the issue elsewhere in the circuit. Hope this information helps.

It's interesting to see relay failures becoming more frequent, especially as more people switch from traditional incandescent and fluorescent bulbs to LED fixtures. The failing relays are often stuck on. Notably, when LEDs replace higher-wattage fixtures and have been switched many times, relays eventually get stuck on. This has been reported in various applications, such as aquatic tank lighting, where users transitioning from fluorescent tubes to LEDs started facing relay issues. The root cause tends to be cheaper LED lights and their electronics, which create large capacitive loads. When relays switch these, they can experience significant current spikes, leading to welded contacts over time. There are several solutions: switch back to incandescent or fluorescent lighting, use a relay with a higher surge rating, or install surge suppressors and snubber networks across the contacts. Some snubber networks allow enough current to light or flicker the LEDs, so they must be carefully designed. Sometimes combining an incandescent with LEDs resolves this. Quality LED fixtures with built-in surge protection are less likely to cause problems. I personally used a small capacitor across my first LED fixture to solve unintended lighting due to snubber current in my hallway when transitioning to LEDs.

Hi, [company_name] offers an inrush current limiter for this purpose. You need one limiter for each relay contact you wish to protect. Hope this provides a solution.

First, I can't get the PT100 temperature input values to display correctly; they're showing as whole values instead of 00.0 format. I have the sensor going through an amplifier to an analog module. Second, for the setpoints: there are three setpoints, VM1, VM2, and VM3. However, adjusting setpoint 2 affects setpoint 1, and changing setpoint 3 affects both 2 and 1, despite there being no programmed link between them. Thanks in advance to anyone who can assist.

Hello [user_name], welcome to the forum. It would help to review your [product_name] web editor project and control program to see what might be causing the issue. Based on your description, it sounds like the web editor doesn't show decimal places for temperature readings, which is a known limitation. [company_name] is aware of this problem but hasn't released a fix yet. Regarding your setpoints: if changing one setpoint affects others, it's likely because the addresses you're using are overlapping. The addressing works at the byte level, and an analog value uses two bytes. For example, if your addresses are VW0, VW1, and VW2, these overlap byte-wise: VW0 uses VB0 and VB1, VW1 uses VB1 and VB2, and VW2 uses VB2 and VB3. This means VB1 is part of both VW0 and VW1, and VB2 is part of both VW1 and VW2, causing the interference you observe. It's best to address words (VW) in steps of two, such as VW0, VW2, VW4, etc.

One more question: what's the difference between 'low word hours counter' and 'high word hours counter'? I need outputs like 'q1', 'q2', 'q3' to indicate which motor (1, 2, or 3) has run for less time than the other two, and I need to adjust the logic.

As mentioned earlier, the operating hours counter outputs a 32-bit value, but [product_name] lets users work only with 16-bit values. To handle this, you need to split the 32-bit (DWord) value into two 16-bit words. For example, let's say you have two counters whose values are stored in the VM area as double word (32-bit) at VD0 and VD4. VD0 contains VW0 (high 16 bits) and VW2 (low 16 bits); VD4 contains VW4 and VW6 similarly. First, compare VW0 and VW4 (the high words) — if VW0 is greater than VW4, then the first meter has a higher value than the second, and you don't need to check the low words. If VW0 and VW4 are equal, then compare the low words (VW2 and VW6) to determine which has run longer.

It seems you misunderstand my instructions. A holding register (HR) has two words (4 bytes). A word in the VM area of [product_name] is 2 bytes. For one HR with 2 words (4 bytes), write them into the VM area sequentially starting from a given address. Example: HR1 (2 words) -> VW1 (start address, uses 2 words). So HR1 goes into VW1+VW2+VW3, and the next available address is VW4, VW5.

It appears the Modbus connection setup is incorrect. For VM mapping, [product_name] is used as server and the Modbus device as client; for NAI mapping, [product_name] is client and Modbus device is server. Your application needs [product_name] to be the client reading from the Modbus server. Try the attached program, which is in diagram mode (easier for single [product_name] setups). Use only locally mapped variables instead of green NAIs. In menu: tools -> ethernet connections -> Connection1 (Modbus Client), the VM mapping is inside. A float requires 2 registers (4 bytes); for example, map to VM0 (uses VB0-VB3, VW0 and VW2). For double, 4 registers (8 bytes)—increase mapped registers if needed. To read several registers in sequence, simply alter the read/write word count. For example, 6 registers (for 3 floats starting at HR500) mapped to VW0 correspond to VM0, VM4, VM8. Adjust the HR and ID (27?) as needed and the correct value should appear in the display.

The main challenge is locating all relevant information. Details of the controller are in the online help or instruction manual for [product_name]. Start by understanding variable memory—this is a byte area from VB0 to VB850. Prefer even numbering (VW0, VW2, VW4) for words as each takes two bytes (VW0=VB0+VB1). For double words, use quad numbering (VD0, VD4, VD8), each is four bytes (VD0 uses VW0+VW2 or VB0+VB1+VB2+VB3). Use the memory as needed but avoid overlapping areas. Learn about Modbus registers via search engines and the Modbus device manual's value table. Many Modbus devices begin at register 0 while [product_name] starts at 1, so often there's a +1 offset. Additional notes: HR (holding registers) for read/write of stored/calculated values, IR (input register) for analog input reads, Coil for read/write bits (status or commands), DI for digital input bits, etc. This is a broad topic—there's always more to learn.

Hi [user_name], I’ve shared information in the German section about motivations for sorting block numbers and the procedure for doing so: "Notes on sorting blocks whose parameters can be edited in RUN mode." The main reasons are easier direct programming on [product_name] modules, improved documentation, and more effective use of parameter assignment mode during program execution. Parameter changes are possible as long as default protection mode remains active. However, blocks in this mode are sorted only by their numbers (not names or types), which can hinder efficient parameter editing, especially for function groups. [user_name] is correct: block numbers cannot be changed via program functions, only manually. Here are some methods, but planning is necessary: 0) You only need sorted block numbers for parameter editing; blocks with protection mode disabled are ignored. 1) If you have spare blocks, insert dummy blocks to push numbering up, then create the sequence you want. 2) If no spare blocks are available, carefully use free numbers within the range, filling gaps with dummy blocks if needed, then rebuilding your program. 3) For larger changes, start a new program, planning the block arrangement with dummy blocks and then transferring necessary blocks across, reconnecting and setting parameters as needed. Keep in mind that analog outputs are always active power sources and remain connected to their terminals, even if set to 0V. These outputs continually try to maintain the specified voltage or current. Picture two batteries connected in parallel with a resistor and a voltmeter. If the resistor becomes zero ohms, the batteries would oppose each other, causing heat and potential damage as the resulting voltage wouldn't be simply 5V or 1V. Hello! Isn't the cable resistance compensation in a 3-wire setup sufficient? You can also eliminate the cable resistance effect by programming an offset to correct it.

Hello [user_name]! Typically, a 3-wire Pt100 connection is adequate for minimizing lead resistance, although there are practical limitations. Within the AM2 PT100 or RTD modules, a Wheatstone Bridge configuration is used along with a microcontroller to handle calculations and compensation per sensor channel. The sensor acts as a resistor forming part of this bridge, and the controller adjusts for resistance changes to maintain balance. The resulting small signals are then passed to [product_name]. If your wiring runs through harsh conditions with substantial temperature changes, the lead resistance may exceed what the internal controller can compensate for and you may get incorrect readings. Since lead resistance is influenced by temperature, conductor size, and length, consider using thicker wires for longer runs, as you cannot control the temperature gradients along the cable. As another user said, it is worth testing with your specific setup to determine what result you get.

Hello, This is a drawback of working in ladder logic compared to function block diagram. Internal markers (flags) are used to complete one relay coil line and then use the result as a normally closed contact on another line. These flags operate internally. In function block diagram, direct graphical connections eliminate the need for such markers. To use internal markers in ladder logic, add a coil and then select 'IM' from the dropdown or type it at the top of the list. There are no restrictions on the number of internal markers, but you need to keep track of which numbers you are using. In my opinion, programming with function block diagram is much simpler than with ladder logic. Hope this helps.

Hello, Could you share more details? Specifically: 1) Does your stepper motor have an integrated controller that can simply receive up/down signals? If not, you might consider using a regular motor with gears. 2) How will you select the desired position—via a rotary switch or time-based control? Describe your stepping cycle. 3) Using a fast counter input to register encoder pulses can help track position, counting up or down as needed. Be sure to include a counter reset (for example, activate a full closed limit switch and press a reset to set the counter to zero). Please provide this information so I can assist further.

Hello, Generally, combining stepper motors directly with [product_name] is not feasible. Stepper motors need a minimum start/stop frequency, which [product_name] can't supply. The maximum output frequency is determined by the scan time—typically 0.1ms per function block, so for 200 function blocks, the scan time is about 20ms (resulting in roughly 50Hz frequency for transistor outputs). Relay outputs are much slower, maxing at 0.5Hz. Instead, consider using an external stepper drive that can be programmed for your five target positions and speed settings, and trigger these via digital input signals. Some manufacturers offer such stepper drives. Hope this provides clarity.

For your question, the maximum resolution for PT100 sensors using the [company_name] module is 0.25 K, as specified in the manual. In the properties of the 'analog amplifier' block, select PT100 as the sensor. The software scales gain and offset for use with PT100 plus module. Mark the option for x 0.1, change decimal points from '0' to '1', and a textbox will show values in the format xxx,n. Note: all block parameters using this scaled value need to be multiplied by 10 (values appear as xxxn). This is [company_name]'s official method for PT100 scaling but it's not fully accurate. For more exact scaling, use two amplifiers in sequence with these settings: 1) gain = 10, offset = 0; 2) gain = 2.5, offset = -5000. Use two decimal digits in your textboxes. Remember to multiply block parameters by 100 now. Your format will be xxx,nn °C on text displays and xxxnn in block values. This way, you achieve 0.25°C resolution accurately. When you turn OFF the power, all standard settings and the program remain in the controller. So after powering ON, it will operate as it did before shutting down. Only blocks with retentive mode enabled will keep their values from before the power OFF; all other values reset to those in the original program. Hello experts, In my current project, I'm working with a pressure transmitter (4-20mA input scaling to 0-16 Bar). I need to switch a digital output on when the line pressure exceeds 4 Bar. I've used an analog amplifier to scale my input, and a comparator to check the value. The comparator activates when the pressure is above 4 Bar, but it remains activated even after the pressure drops. I'm seeking advice on properly comparing analog values and on resetting the comparator output. My tests were done in simulation and I've attached the relevant program. Kind regards

Hello, The issue is with the SF002 configuration—you need to set separate ON and OFF values. Using distinct values introduces hysteresis, which is beneficial because analog signals tend to fluctuate. For example, if the ON threshold is 4 Bar and the input oscillates between 4.01 and 3.98, the output will continuously switch, causing instability. I also updated the scaling by multiplying by 10 for improved accuracy.

The analog inputs on the basic modules of [product_name] only process 0-10V voltage signals, not current signals. If you want to use a 4-20mA signal on the analog inputs, you’ll need to either use an external transmitter that converts 4-20mA to 0-10V, or use a 500-ohm precision resistor (1% tolerance, minimum 0.5 watts) as a load to convert the current into a 2-10V voltage drop, which the analog input can then read.

Hello everyone, The [product_name] [article_no] introduces several new function blocks. I’d like to share a practical evaluation of the “average” block here: The “average” block calculates a periodic average over a number of past values. While this is technically feasible, using all analog inputs within reasonable circuit complexity only allows up to n = 32 values (with an entry value range from 0 to 1000). Despite these limitations, the block is impressive – according to the manual, n can be up to 32767 (depending on sampling time), and each entry value can cover the full analog range from -32768 to 32767. A drawback is that the minimal total sampling time (St) is just 1 second, meaning measurements are spaced by St/SN. Using this block for analog input signals requires paying attention to these constraints, as low scanning rates may lead to undetected measurement errors or inaccurate block results. For previous versions like [product_name] [article_no], there was a way to filter analog display values in text messages, though this also risked low scanning frequencies. Similar filter blocks can help make displayed values appear more stable, but this isn’t ideal when those values are needed for further calculations. It’s clear that changes in analog input updates controlled by [product_name] hardware could lower the scanning rate, but this can’t be adjusted further within the system. In general, reducing scan or update frequency should be avoided to ensure digitized analog signals are as accurate as possible. Unfortunately, block parameters cannot be defined by reference. Block behavior when activating the “EN” and “R” input pins: - If entry “R” is enabled, the block skips the current sampling time and ignores the output. - If “EN” is set to “0” briefly, sampling is paused (but not reset). This means you cannot restart sampling without clearing the output, which hinders potential mid-cycle adjustments or alignments. Additionally, circuit designs reusing the block’s output must account for the output being forced to zero during St instead of retaining the previous measured value. Summary: As an alternative (to previously published circuits), the “average” block (available only on [product_name] [article_no]) can filter analog inputs, provided these parameter requirements are met: - St / SN = 0.300 s (Basic module analog inputs) - St / SN = 0.050 s (Expansion module analog inputs) Best regards, [user_name]

You can set the IP address and subnet mask directly on the device, but only in administrator mode. PSTN/Fixed Line Remote Service ========================= A similar method was demonstrated for [product_name] back in October 2003 for [article_no] (refer to attached zip file). The documentation outlines some insights on communication—like how crossover Tx & Rx means modem DCE to [product_name] DTE, and how modem AT command settings are relevant. This process was later replaced with the Modem Cable and Wizard in [product_name] V6, but essentially, the fundamental checks remain—review COM port settings and validate the modem cable with a multimeter. GSM-Based Remote Service ===================== This has been an ongoing topic. Here are some details I've gathered, hoping others might contribute more experiences or information. I've investigated this for several years and identified three main challenges: 1) 11-bit GSM modem support Although this is typically cited as the primary issue, other factors may also contribute. Most GSM modems support only 10-bit character framing such as 8N1 or 7E1 (with configurations for start bit, data bits, parity, and stop bit). Some modems can be configured with AT commands to change this setup, and a few even allow 11-bit communication on the RS232 side (PC & [product_name] interface) while maintaining 10-bit communication over GSM. Many modem manufacturers use a 'wireless module' or 'cellular engine' from companies like: - [company_name] (now Centerion) - Wavecom/Sierra Wireless - Sagem - Motorola - Telit - Sony Ericsson Check whether these support 11-bit protocol and how to configure their AT commands accordingly. [product_name] typically requires 8E1 industrial framing (start bit, 8 data bits, EVEN parity, and stop bit), offering basic error detection and correction. Some industrial modems are capable of 11-bit framing (see attached file), though I haven’t personally tested or verified their internal modules. 2) Synchronous vs. Asynchronous Communication Synchronous communication uses extra handshaking lines for the devices to synchronize clocks and coordinate data transmission statuses. Asynchronous methods do not synchronize transfer rates, requiring one side to interpret the flow and timing of bits without explicit coordination. More details can be found in the attached document and further explained through external sources like Wikipedia. Adapter wiring suggests asynchronous communication, though specific AT modem settings may introduce some confusion. See attached documentation for more details. 3) Transparent vs. Non-Transparent Data Transfer Excerpts from a cellular provider (included in the documentation) help explain this further. The Radio Link Protocol (RLP) used in non-transparent mode introduces network-based error correction, which could impact communication reliability with [product_name]. Non-transparent communication employs RLP for enhanced error correction and data integrity, utilizing acknowledgement signals and buffering to ensure an uninterrupted transmission. Transparent data, on the other hand, means no additional GSM-side error correction. Not all cellphones and modems support non-transparent (RLP-based) transmission. Faxing standards (Group 3) use transparent protocols. That’s all for now—please share any further clarifications or experiences.

When selecting your [product_name], how do you decide between relay contacts or transistor outputs?

This choice depends entirely on your specific application.

Transistor outputs provide a fixed output voltage, usually matching the supply voltage of the [product_name], for example 24VDC. Relay contacts, on the other hand, are potential-free, meaning they aren't tied to the [product_name] power supply and can be used with various voltages as needed. For example, you could connect Q1 to 230VAC, Q2 to 24VDC, and Q3 to 12VAC, depending on your requirements. Transistor outputs offer faster switching (such as for PWM applications), operate silently, and feature internal current limiting for protection, while relays can be heard when switching.

Hello, sorry for my basic question, but could someone clarify what exactly an open connector is and in which situations I should use it? Thanks in advance.

Did you check the help section for the block? Everything is explained there. Some blocks require the output to be connected even if you don't actually use the output. That's when open connectors are needed. If the output isn't connected, you won't be able to upload the software to the device. For example, with the message block, leaving the output unconnected causes an error when uploading. Connecting the output to an open connector resolves the issue and lets everything work.

Hi [user_name], thanks for your feedback. Let me explain the reason open connectors are required! [product_name] function blocks operate on a platform similar to Java, where each block has multiple inputs and always exactly one output, even if it’s just a message text. Successful execution of a function block requires that all inputs and outputs are defined or terminated. The open connector is used to terminate an output that doesn't need to be connected elsewhere. Outputs, digital markers, and analog flags can also serve as terminators but are best not used, as it wastes valuable programming resources. In simulation mode on a PC, terminations are less critical because the thread environment handles everything. However, on the microcontroller inside the [product_name], missing terminations will prevent download or compilation because the thread environment expects definitions for all outputs. If you run out of open connectors, you can use OR gates in a cascade to have one open connector serve multiple terminations. For analog signals, you can use an analog threshold trigger as a placeholder, with its output tied to an open connector. While it may seem inefficient, this method works. I heard at a recent trade fair that the next [product_name] will offer more open connectors, making things simpler. Happy programming!

If I understand correctly, you want the output Q1 to be ON when the temperature is below 25°C, and OFF when it's above 25°C, right? Here's what I suggest: Set your analog amplifier with Gain: 1.5, Offset: -500, and Decimal places: 1. This gives you a temperature range of -50.0°C to 100.0°C, making temperature control easier. For the threshold trigger, set ON at 250, OFF at 240, with Decimal places: 1. Add a NOT block between the threshold trigger and output Q1. This setup provides a hysteresis of 1.0°C. If the temperature drops below 24.0°C, Q1 switches ON. When it rises above 25.0°C, Q1 switches OFF. If it falls below 24.0°C again, Q1 will turn back ON.

That's exactly what I needed. Now everything works as intended. Thank you for helping to resolve the issue quickly.

Hello [user_name], The 0–10 V DC analog inputs on [product_name] or its AM2 expansion module cannot connect directly to a load cell. The device samples and digitizes input signals, providing 10-bit resolution (0–1000 value). Only voltage changes greater than 0.01 V (10 mV) are detected, so very small load cell signals won't be recognized due to insufficient resolution. Load cells typically use a Wheatstone Bridge configuration and require stable temperature for accurate measurement, along with signal amplification. [product_name] does not have a built-in load cell module for this. You may need an external load cell module that balances the bridge and outputs an amplified signal (e.g., 0–10 V, 0–20 mA, or 4–20 mA) proportional to weight. This signal can then be processed by [product_name] or AM2 for scaling and display. Hope this explanation is helpful!

Hello [user_name], I've noticed in your example, when running a simulation or deploying on the controller, the value of B005 Random generator is retained and immediately written to AM1 when restarted. It doesn't reset to zero as expected. How can I ensure everything starts from zero?

B005 only sets the interval for the next random value, ensuring a new value for each interval. Thus, the total time of TH+TL of B005 should never be less than TH of B001. The actual randomization occurs in B001. When the controller starts, AQ1 outputs zero. B001 then provides a new random value, so it won’t reset to zero when toggling between slider and random. To implement an on/off function, replace B003’s permanent activation with an input. Best regards, [user_name]

Hello, Only the [product_name] 24RCE or 24RCEo supports both configurations. Unlike your current [product_name] model, this version uses relay outputs instead of transistors. Since the 24RCE/o model supports 24V AC & DC, you can wire it to read M-signals.

Hi, thanks for the response. The units I have are [article_no]. Can I confirm that this type only allows one wiring method? The [product_name] 12/24 lacks sink/source selection, only supporting PNP logic. For a high input signal, you need a connection to L+. What works is to connect your NPN logic to the input and add a pull-up resistor (such as 1kOhm) from the input to L+. You need the output specs of the signals to choose the correct resistor value. Regards, [user_name]

To cover a distance of 4 km, a radio link is needed, but keep in mind that the farther the distance, the lower the bandwidth with typical frequencies. For example, a 2.4 GHz connection typically reaches only 300m, while 869 MHz can reach 3,000m but may not have enough bandwidth for [product_name] or software like [product_name] Soft Comfort. Modbus connections might be an option. Depending on terrain, repeaters may be required, and line-of-sight and weather play a big role. If you only need to check a sensor value, wireless Modbus sensors could be more practical, though they can be costly – expect to spend around 3,000 euros. Specialists from Schildknecht have experience assisting with radio link selection. For tank sensors, consider what the tank is made of, the type of liquid, and the maximum fill height. For tanks that don't freeze, tachometers or pressure sensors are suitable; ultrasonic or radar sensors often struggle with condensation. Monitoring tanks that freeze is difficult – pressure sensors may get damaged by ice. From my experience, I often use sensors from brands like Peppler & Fuchs, E&H, IFM, or [company_name]. There are several ways to transmit data from [product_name] over such a distance. If mobile service is available at your location, you could use a mobile communication module or interface module for [product_name]. Some modules allow a connection to the built-in web server where you can access data remotely, provided you have a SIM card with a public IP address. The same hardware can also send SMS notifications. Alternatively, certain modules allow data to be forwarded to AWS cloud dashboards, eliminating the need for a public IP. SMS notifications for power status are also supported. If mobile coverage isn’t available, some Wi-Fi routers permit longer distance connections, though in Europe the range is limited to about 300 meters and in the USA sometimes extends miles. Radio modems have also been used for such distances, but you must comply with local regulations regarding radio transmissions. Power line modems, which use the electrical network, could be another solution, though their effective range may not reach 3,000 meters. Good luck.

It's difficult to give a definite answer without seeing your actual program. In any case, VM memory in [product_name] is not persistent.

This program.

Ha, ha, ha... that's a good joke. You've misunderstood something. In VM byte 0 (VB0), which you use for the weekday parameterization of the weekly timer, bits V0.0 to V0.7 correspond (V0.0 - V0.7). Yes, that setup is fine. When the sensor is not triggered, its output is open and the 2.2k resistor pulls input I1 to 24VDC, making I1 HIGH. When the sensor is triggered, the output closes and input I1 goes to 0V (M), making I1 LOW.

You have flexibility in resistor values and can calculate for the following: 1) Low level = NO contact closed; resistor should not exceed the maximum sensor output current (U/I=R, so 24V/0.3A=80 Ohm). 2) High level = NO contact open; the external resistor is in series with the controller's input resistor (~70kOhm), and sufficient voltage is needed for input HIGH. Values between 1kOhm and 10kOhm provide a good margin for both, so nothing will be damaged. Check operation instructions for required low and high levels of the inputs. With a 10kOhm resistor in series with ~70kOhm input, you get about 21V at the input. Regards, [user_name]

Hello everyone, To compare constant values (less than 19999) with an analog value efficiently, you can use a block like an "analog threshold trigger". Below are general techniques for testing an analog value Ax against a constant n (which can be zero): A) To test if Ax equals n: Configure the block parameters as GAIN = 1.0, OFFSET = 0; Threshold ON = n, Threshold OFF = n + 1. For example, if n = 0: ON = 0; OFF = 1. Q output is ON when Ax = 0. B) To check if Ax is greater than n: Set GAIN = 1.0, OFFSET = 0; Threshold ON = OFF = n. If n = 0: ON = 0; OFF = 0. Q output is ON when Ax > 0. This works as a positive number test. C) To check if Ax is less than n: Set GAIN = -1.0, OFFSET = 0; Threshold ON = OFF = -n. For n = 0: GAIN = -1.0; ON = 0; OFF = 0. Q output is ON when Ax < 0. This tests for negative values. D) For Ax >= n: Use GAIN = 1.0, OFFSET = 0; Threshold ON = n, Threshold OFF = n - 1. For n = 2: ON = 2; OFF = 3. Q output is ON when Ax >= 2. E) For Ax <= n: Set GAIN = -1.0, OFFSET = 0; Threshold ON = -n; Threshold OFF = -n - 1. For n = 2: GAIN = -1.0; ON = -2; OFF = -3. Q output is ON when Ax <= 2. With this block, you can also check if an analog value falls inside a range (ON = k1 - 1, OFF = k2, within limits -20000 to 20000). For values or ranges outside this domain, use a "comparator" block in analog mode for direct comparison between two analog values. Guidance for comparing two analog values is available at [url]. Additionally, there is an extended circuit for broader use along with parameter explanations. Please refer to the example circuit "[document]" attached. Best regards, [user_name]

Hello, This is a feature of [product_name] programming that prevents direct recursive connections (connecting an output back to an input earlier in the path) unless you use a Flag (M bit) or a hardware output. You can check page 63 of the [product_name] manual for guidance on 'The four Golden rules for operating [product_name]'; notably, Rule 2 states: Rule 2: Outputs and inputs - Always build your circuit from output to input. You can connect one output to multiple inputs, but not one input to multiple outputs. You cannot connect an output upstream to an input in the same program path; for such internal loops, use flags or outputs. Best regards, [user_name]

Hello everyone. I want to load a program from an SD card every time the controller boots. If the SD card is missing during boot, the program shouldn't run. At the same time, the SD card should be copy protected. Is this possible? Thank you.

No, that's not possible. When the controller restarts, it checks for an SD card with a program. If a valid program is found, it checks whether it's different from the one in flash memory. If so, it loads the program from the SD card to flash memory. But once the program is loaded into flash, the SD card can be removed—the device no longer requires it. There is no setting that forces the controller to only operate when the SD card is present.

Hi, You can try the following steps, but ensure you have a backup of the [product_name] Soft Comfort program: - Download the program to the controller. - In the controller's settings, go to the SD card menu and activate copy protection. - Copy the program from the controller to the SD card. - Copy the program back from the SD card to the controller. After removing the SD card, the controller should display 'No program.' Even with the card removed and power cycled, the controller will show 'No program' and won't execute anything. This solution mostly addresses your requirements, but the SD card needs to remain inserted at all times. You could also set a program password. That way, if the SD card is removed and connected to a PC, the program can still be accessed if the password is known. Hope this helps.

From the manual: [product_name] provides a 1024-byte buffer for data logging. When the buffer reaches 512 bytes, data is written to the micro SD card. If data is generated faster than it can be written, data loss may occur. To prevent this, ensure the enable signal for the data log block is triggered no more frequently than every 500 ms. Without a micro SD card, only 512 bytes can be stored, and excess data is lost. All parameterized values are logged, regardless of whether changes have been made.

Hello, Based on my experience with data logging in [product_name] version_no, a 10 ms pulse at the data log block input is sufficient for recording. So a generator with 10 ms ON and 29.9 seconds OFF should work; otherwise, try increasing the pulse width to 100 ms. Regarding logging: every positive edge at the ENABLE input of the data log block records all configured data, independent of signal or value changes. For triggered recording, you can use an OR gate to combine the trigger signal and pulse generator, allowing both cyclic and event-based logging. Hope this helps.

I'm planning to create a small home automation setup using [product_name]. I want the system to have backup power in case of a main power failure. I've discovered some [company_name] DC UPS modules with maintenance-free battery modules. My goal is to minimize power consumption during outages. Hi [user_name], Initially, I didn't think this approach was feasible because of the required power-up sequence for both the [product_name] and its expansion modules. The documentation indicates that expansion modules must receive power before—or exactly at the same time as—the [product_name] base unit (CPU). Since the [product_name] takes several seconds to boot, both can get power at once, and when the CPU checks for modules, they're already powered. If power is supplied to expansion modules only after the CPU has finished booting up, the communication LEDs will remain red, signaling no connection from the left side. This happens because the CPU didn't detect any expansion modules at startup, so it's not communicating actively. However, after some testing, I found that if the full rack/configuration has been successfully powered on once, it's possible to remove power from expansion modules while the CPU keeps running, and reapply power later—communication resumes to all modules. I tried this setup with a CPU and several expansion modules, all at 24 VDC. This allows the CPU to establish bus communication, and expansion modules reconnect when powered up again. However, please note: 1) This may not work with communication modules (KNX/EIB or AS-i). 2) My tests are only with 24 VDC modules/CPUs—not 230V AC. 3) Unexpected behavior may occur in your running program—the CPU might read changed input states due to switching. 4) Warranty may be affected by repeatedly switching modules like this. 5) [company_name] likely doesn't recommend or approve this method! 6) Do not attempt in explosive environments—there's a risk of sparks when modules power up again. Keep in mind, expansion modules draw their highest current when all relays are activated, or when analog outputs are fully engaged. Good luck with your project!

[product_name] analog inputs accept standard signals such as 0-10V or 0-20mA. These inputs may come from sensors with different ranges and units, so scaling is required to reflect the actual range of physical signals. To scale: If your physical signal is between values a and b, you need to convert your input (0-10) to match this range (a-b). To do this, calculate the correct gain and offset: gain = (b - a) / 10 (for 0-10V signals), offset = a. For 0-20mA inputs, the process is similar, involving a linear relationship between input and scaled signal. Refer to [product_name] help for more details.

Keep in mind that [product_name] uses 1-based Modbus addressing, while the Waveshare module uses 0-based addressing. The first address for Waveshare is 0, so accessing HR0 from [product_name] requires HR1 in the connection table. Based on the byte count, you're referencing a MODBUS TCP frame. The breakdown is as follows: 00 00 (Transaction Identifier, 2 bytes); 00 00 (Protocol Identifier, 2 bytes); 00 06 (Length Field, 2 bytes); 01 (Unit Identifier, 1 byte); 05 (Function Code - 'Write Single Coil', 1 byte); 00 00 (Coil Address, 2 bytes); FF 00 (Coil Value, 2 bytes - turns the coil on). For more details, consult the protocol documentation.

The Modbus connection table contains these entries: VW0 - 2 Words - HR1 - 2 Words; VW2 - 2 Words - HR3 - 2 Words. The first entry writes VW0 and VW2 to HR1 and HR2, while the second entry writes VW2 and VW4 to HR3 and HR4. Holding Registers and VW variables are both words (16 bits), but HR addressing is word-based while VW is byte-based. For example: HR1, HR2, HR3, HR4... VW0, VW2, VW4, VW6... So the increment for VW addresses should be 2 instead of 1, as in the case for HR.

Hi, Your setup isn't correct. The memory within [product_name] is organized by bytes. Your configuration is: VW1 consists of VB1 & VB2, and VW2 consists of VB2 & VB3, which causes overlapping of memory addresses. The [product_name] memory space ranges from address VB0 to VB850. So for VM-Mapping, use VW0, VW2, and VW4, and match these addresses in your cloud data configuration table. Also, you can't write to your current data configuration. You can spot this by looking at the marking in the VM-mapping table. If you want write access, the 'Parameter' column marking should show a paper and pen symbol, not a circle. Problem 2: "Unable to assume role aws-elasticbeanstalk-service-role." (Environment stuck in Warning/Pending) Go to IAM Console > Roles > Create role. Select "AWS service" then "Elastic Beanstalk" (choose the Environment management use case). Ensure the AWSElasticBeanstalkService policy (or automatically selected policies, such as AWSElasticBeanstalkEnhancedHealth and [BINARY_DATA_REMOVED]) are attached. Name the role: aws-elasticbeanstalk-service-role. Hopefully, these tips help others save time.

Hello, How many expansion modules can be connected to a [product_name]? Can different module types be used together, for example combining a [product_name] digital module with an analog module? Currently, I have a [product_name] base module and notice on the display labels such as: I1, I2= AI3, AI4 (0..10V), I7, I8= AI1, AI2 (0..10V). What do these labels indicate?

Hi, Please review the compatibility overview of [product_name] base modules and their expansion modules for more information. Best regards, [user_name]

Hi! You can physically attach a large number of expansion modules and create a very extended [product_name] configuration; however, the software only supports: - 24 digital inputs (channels, not modules) - 16 digital outputs - 8 analog inputs - 2 analog outputs If you connect the maximum permitted digital I/O modules (for example, 4 digital modules with 8 channels each or 2 with 16 channels, subject to supply voltage), the last 4 digital outputs cannot be controlled via software. This is due to limitations in the expansion bus communication and synchronisation, and changing it would cause older modules to lose compatibility. If you use on-board digital inputs as analog inputs (0..10V) on modules like [product_name] base modules, you can only add a limited number of expansion analog input modules (up to 3 if using 2 on-board analog, up to 2 if using all 4 on-board analog). These can be configured in the software settings. When using on-board digital inputs as analog, you can't use the same input numbers for digital handling in your program, reducing usable digital inputs. If additional modules such as communication or network modules are added, physical digital and analog inputs/outputs need to be available for mapping. As for the label question, the display tells you that certain digital inputs (such as I1, I2, I7, I8) can be used as analog inputs (AI1–AI4) depending on module version. The numbering is designed to maintain compatibility with older designs and programs. Hope this helps clarify things and supports any diagrams or reference material you’ve seen. Cheers, [user_name]

A simple approach is to activate a timer (for example, an on-delay timer) using the output of the threshold trigger. Set the timer to measure in 1/100 second intervals, with a maximum delay of 99 seconds, and display the timer's current value on the screen. As long as the output signal stays on for less than 99 seconds, the timer will show the elapsed time while the output is active.

There is a challenge here: [product_name] does not have a built-in stopwatch feature. You can start and stop a timer (like an on-delay) with a threshold, but stopping the timer resets its value to zero, so you only see time while it’s running. What you likely need is a custom stopwatch. There was a solution shared on the German forum (thanks to [user_name]). Please check the attached [document]. You just need to adjust the minimum and maximum values for the analog threshold triggers B016 and B018, and consider when to reset the timer (input I3)—perhaps when pressure drops below 1.5 bar. To use the stopwatch without an analog value, I kept inputs I1 and I2.

Hello, I'm new to PI controllers and I'm having trouble understanding something. I set up a small test to learn how a PI controller works, with the setpoint at 200 and the direction set to upwards (+). The PI controller in [product_name] only operates in one direction at a time, so you need to select the appropriate control direction. For upward control direction (Dir = +): If the process value drops below the setpoint, the controller reacts and tries to bring the process value back up to the setpoint. If the process value goes above the setpoint, the controller does not respond. For downward control direction (Dir = -): If the process value exceeds the setpoint, the controller adjusts and tries to bring the process value back down to the setpoint. If the process value is less than the setpoint, the controller does not respond.

Thanks for the explanation, I got the directions mixed up. However, I'm still unclear about your statement regarding the controller not working when the process value exceeds the setpoint for positive direction or falls below for negative direction. The PI controller's output never goes below zero—it ranges from 0 to 1000. For upward control: If the process value is less than the setpoint, the controller gives an output between 0 and 1000. If the process value goes above the setpoint, the output drops to 0. For downward control: If the process value exceeds the setpoint, the output is between 0 and 1000. If the process value is below the setpoint, the output drops to 0. Does this clarify the behavior?

I understand your point. For example, with negative direction, the output ranges only from 0 to 1000. If the process value rises above the setpoint, the output increases. If the process value matches the setpoint again, the output stays at its last value. However, when the process value falls below the setpoint, the output doesn't instantly go to zero; it gradually decreases, and if the process value returns to the setpoint before reaching zero, the output stabilizes at that last value, as far as I know.

The addressing of analog inputs for the expansion module depends on several factors. In the configuration file settings, under offline I/O options, you control how many analog inputs are enabled on the base module. By default, two analog inputs are available, addressed as AI1 (I7) and AI2 (I8). The first analog expansion module uses: Channel 1 = AI3 Channel 2 = AI4 If the base module has no analog inputs activated, the expansion takes addresses AI1 and AI2. With two analog inputs enabled on the base, the module starts at AI3 and AI4. If four analog inputs are enabled, the expansion's inputs begin at AI5 and AI6.

[product_name] 24RCE does not include onboard analog inputs. Thus, the addresses for the first analog expansion module will be AI1 and AI2.

Hello, The analog input shows values from 0 to 1000, which corresponds to a voltage range of 0 to 10V. This means the smallest step you can measure is 10V divided by 1000 digits, which equals 0.01V per digit. No matter how you scale or multiply, the lowest voltage change the system detects on an analog input is 0.01V. Hope this answers your question.

Hello [user_name], Unfortunately, the system can only measure down to 0.01V, and you require 0.001V resolution, so it's not possible to achieve the accuracy you need. If you use a highly accurate amplifier before the input to convert your 1-2V signal into a 0-10V signal, you may get closer. However, the amplifier must be very linear, and the system input itself typically does not perform better than about 0.02V ± 1 bit, and may vary more (there might be documentation about this, but I can't locate it right now). Therefore, achieving a true 0.001V reading is not possible with this setup. I have used a Weidmuller module for a similar task on the system, but the required accuracy was lower than yours.

Welcome to the forum. If the voltage at a digital input is less than 5 VDC, it's detected as a low (0) signal. For voltages above 12 VDC, it's considered a high (1) signal. The highest permissible voltage at an input is 28.8 VDC. The [product_name] base module only evaluates voltage at its inputs—not current. Additionally, on base modules powered by 12 VDC or 24 VDC, four inputs can function as analog inputs (within 0-10 VDC range).

Thanks for the explanation! So the input current spec just ensures enough sink current for ON/OFF operation, but it's not a specification for current input, correct? If my input voltage ranges from 18-36 VDC, I would need to scale it down appropriately. Is that sufficient?

All inputs can handle a maximum of 28.8 VDC between the supply voltage minus (M) and plus terminals, with M set at 0 VDC.

Avoid using input voltages between 5 and 12 VDC. In this range, the input may unpredictably be detected as either a 0 or a 1, so it's not reliable.

According to the specifications, the [product_name] RTD module only supports PT100 sensors within a temperature range of -50°C to 200°C. I need to measure a boiler's internal temperature up to 450°C, which requires a higher-range PT100 sensor. Online, there are many PT100 sensors available that cover temperatures from -20°C to 400/450°C. How can I connect a PT100 sensor rated up to 450°C to the [product_name] RTD module with a 200°C limit? Or is there an alternative way to use these higher-temperature PT100 sensors?

Are you certain the sensor is actually a PT type? Try measuring both the temperature and the resistance at the sensor. Comparing the resistance value at the measured temperature against a PT100 table will confirm whether the sensor is truly a PT100.

Hello, I currently have three RTD modules connected to standard PT100 sensors and everything works fine within the 200°C range. I haven't purchased a 450°C sensor yet, but I'm searching for one similar to those found on auction sites: [url]. Do you think these are real PT100 sensors? They also offer a version labeled 'K' with a range of -50°C to 450°C. Can this PT100 sensor be connected?

A PT100 sensor functions as a resistor that changes value based on temperature. The PT sensor you are considering should operate in the -50°C to 400°C range. When connected to the [product_name] RTD module, only resistance values corresponding to -50°C to 200°C are interpreted; temperatures above 200°C will be displayed as 200°C by the module. To cover the range from -50°C to 400°C, you'll need an external temperature transmitter that outputs a signal such as 0 to 10V or 0/4 to 20mA. Note that a sensor labeled 'K' refers to a thermocouple, not a PT sensor, and can't be used directly. For thermocouples, you would require an external transmitter and appropriate compensation wiring.

Thank you for the example, it works well. How did you determine the mapping for virtual words and double words? For instance, Counter 1 is mapped to VD10, VD14, VD18 & VD22. How was this decided? Was there a [document] from [company_name]? Similarly for timers, T002 is mapped to VW26, VW28 & VW30, and T003 to VW32, VW34 & VW36.

The mapping in the VM area is structured by bytes. Bit: Vx.y, where x is the byte number and y is the bit number in the byte. For example, V9.4 is byte 9, bit 4. A byte consists of 8 bits; VB0 covers V0.0 to V0.7. A word is 2 consecutive bytes; VW0 covers VB0 and VB1. A DWord is 2 consecutive words; VD0 covers VW0 and VW2 (VB0 to VB3). The VM area contains 851 bytes, from VB0 to VB850.

Is the assignment sequence 'top down' or 'first in, first out'? Does C0001 start at VD10 because that's the first item read by the controller in the ladder code? If T002 was T001 (and C0001 was C0002), would it start at V10?

No, the addresses can be freely assigned. Just make sure not to duplicate or overlap assignments. For example, if you use bit signals V0.0 - V0.3, do not use VB0, VW0, or VD0 to avoid conflicts.

Hi, Generally, I am aware of three situations where the USB programming cable may not work: 1. Incorrect cable installation (connecting the cable to the PC before installing the driver). Please refer to the [company_name] FAQ to resolve this. 2. Incompatible or outdated driver for the USB cable. Make sure you use the latest version from the [company_name] website. See: [url] 3. The USB driver may assign a high virtual COM port number, or active Bluetooth devices may conflict. Check in the system control panel under device manager, Ports (COM and LPT), and locate the relevant USB-to-UART Bridge. If Bluetooth devices are enabled, up to 10 COM ports may already be assigned. Installing the USB cable after these devices can result in the software scanning all available COM ports, potentially taking a long time or failing to find the correct port. To resolve this: 1. Uninstall the driver for the USB cable. Optionally, remove Bluetooth devices if unnecessary, then reinstall the USB driver. 2. If Bluetooth devices are still needed, try to assign a COM port below the Bluetooth range: Go to device manager and select the correct USB-to-UART Bridge, then open properties, tap the settings, and under advanced, change to a free port number (typically 4 and above, as lower ones may be reserved). After this, open the programming software, go to Tools > Options > Interface and let it search for the correct COM port. These steps should assist. Please note, information about the USB cable's COM port is only available when it's connected to the PC. Hope this helps.

Hello everyone, I'm new to this forum and looking for advice. I have a [product_name] base module ([article_no]) and want to display a fluid level measured by a variable resistance probe (range: 33 ohm to 240 ohm). I also have the [product_name] RTD module for temperature readings and the standard analog module for voltage/current measurements. High precision isn't essential. Which connection method would you recommend? If I use the PLC's 24VDC, I'd need to add a 350 ohm series resistor, resulting in a voltage reading between 2V and 10V and a maximum current of 62mA, consuming about 1.5W continuously. Is this current too much for the PLC? Alternatively, powering the probe with 5VDC and a 220 ohm series resistor would bring consumption down to 0.1W, or even lower if using a 1.2V battery and a 27 ohm resistor (0.025W). Any suggestions? Thank you.

Welcome to the forum. The best approach is to use a probe with a standard 0-10V or 0/4-20mA output. Other methods with your current probe are more of a workaround and less reliable.

You can generally use your proposed method, but the current going to the PLC may not be as you calculated. Most of the current will pass through the external resistors; the analog input of the base module has a high impedance (~70kOhm). With 24V maximum, current would be roughly 0.34mA. Regarding the resistors: the 350 ohm is on +24V, the 33-240 ohm is on 0V, and the junction between them goes to the analog input (ignore the 70kOhm impedance for calculations). Maximum current is 24/(350+33)=62.7mA, minimum is 24/(350+240)=40.7mA. For power calculations: P=I²xR. 0.0627²x33=0.13W, 0.0407²x240=0.4W. For Umax=10V, you need 0.4W. Check your variable resistor specs for suitability. Also confirm power ratings for the fixed resistor. Remember, resistor values can vary with temperature. Best regards, [user_name]

Thank you for your input, [user_name]. I'm glad our calculations match. The power you calculated is what dissipates in the probe itself. If you also include the 350 ohm series resistor, the total power is roughly 1.5W. How would you suggest connecting this setup to the [product_name]? Also, what are your thoughts on using a 5VDC supply (instead of the PLC's 24V), or even a 1.2V battery, and linking everything to the 4-20mA analog input? Best regards and stay safe.

As previously described, connect the resistors in series from +24V to 0V: first the 350 ohm, then the 33-240 ohm as a voltage divider, with the junction wired to the analog input (for example I7(AI1)). Reducing voltage does decrease power consumption, but may impact resolution. If probe resistor temperature is an issue, increasing the 350 ohm resistor can help, though it will reduce full measurement resolution. Is the relationship between resistance and fluid level linear or not? Nonlinearity could complicate measurements, and using a spreadsheet to visualize this may help. The [product_name] system only supports basic arithmetic; complex approximations require polynomial functions. Best regards, [user_name]

Thank you, [user_name]. I understand the wiring and the trade-off between reduced power and resolution loss by increasing the resistance. I'll consider this topic resolved. Regards to you.

It's recommended to use a dedicated measurement interface and probe designed for liquid level detection. 1. Using DC current may lead to electrical corrosion of the probe. 2. Make sure to install input protection for the PLC to prevent damage from voltage spikes.

Hello everyone, I am attempting to read the date and time from [product_name] using Modbus. According to the [product_name] manual, these are located at VB985...VB990, but I am unable to convert these addresses for Modbus FC3 or FC4 functions. Can someone provide an example? Thank you in advance.

This can be accomplished, but there are limitations. You can access this VM memory area remotely through Modbus, although only by word rather than byte. For this, the holding register function FC3 must be used. You need to read HR492 to HR495. HR492 = VW984 = VB984 + VB985. VB985 contains the year. HR493 = VW986 = VB986 + VB987. VB986 is the month, VB987 is the day. HR494 = VW988 = VB988 + VB989. VB988 stores the hours, VB989 the minutes. HR495 = VW990 = VB990 + VB991. VB990 represents the seconds.

Thank you very much, this solution works perfectly.

The special M8 flag becomes active only after restarting the [product_name] for one cycle at a HIGH state. A program can detect when the [product_name] restarts. That may not be necessary: after some further experimentation I was able to find an answer. For anyone facing similar ladder diagram block counting issues in the future, here’s what I discovered: 1. Make contacts are not counted as blocks 2. Break contacts do count 3. Relay coils appear not to count 4. Using OR contacts increases the block count (the amount depends on how many contacts are involved) 5. Using AND contacts also increases the block count in a similar way If you primarily use ladder diagrams like me, the block counting logic can seem confusing. However, it becomes clearer when viewed in terms of Function Block Diagrams (FBD). For example, when chaining AND or OR operations, you’ll notice limitations — an AND or OR block will only accept a certain number of inputs before you need to link multiple blocks. Official documentation suggests four inputs for AND/OR blocks, but in practice (at least for [article_no]) this seems incorrect.

The VM addresses from 984 to 990 hold bytes for the RTC. VM 985 corresponds to the year in the RTC. Since it uses only one byte, its maximum value is 256. Is it correct that the year in the VM table starts at 2000, so the actual year equals 2000 plus the value in VM985?

The VM byte 985 contains only the last two digits of the full year. The calculation is '20+' plus the value in VM985, meaning a value of 20 in VM985 represents the year 2020. Similarly, if VM985 is 21, it indicates the year 2021.

Hello! [product_name] modules can only handle integers. If you transfer floating point values from another system over the network using the Modbus protocol, [product_name] cannot process them directly. However, by using the Integer/Float Converter function block, you can convert integers to floats by applying a resolution to the value range and store the results in memory. You can then transfer these results over the network. You need to set an appropriate resolution for the output float when configuring parameters. Typically, both the Float/Integer and Integer/Float converter blocks are needed to complete the task. A standard workflow is: 1) Transfer floats from an external system via network (with Modbus protocol) and store them in memory. 2) Use the Float/Integer converter to change floats in memory to integers. 3) Process the integer data in the module. 4) Use the Integer/Float converter to transform the result back to floats and store them. 5) Transfer floats to the external system again via network.

Hello, I'm seeking guidance on the purpose and usage of Flags. I'd also like to know if they operate similarly to VM mapping. Thanks.

Digital flags store the logical state at their input and pass this value to the output in the following cycle. On [product_name] devices, there are usually 64 digital flags, with some reserved for internal system functions. Flags can be used for remote control, and their state can be set to 0 or 1 remotely when not connected to logic inputs. Remote control is also possible via the internal web server. Flags are also essential when you want to avoid recursive operations. Analog flags similarly pass the input value to the output one cycle later. VM mapping serves a different function and is not related to flags.

Can anyone assist with scaling a 4-20 mA analog input for a temperature range of -30°C to +60°C on an [product_name] module?

Please check the attached file for more details.

Thank you very much. Why does this process require two steps? Is it possible to achieve this with greater precision, for instance with one decimal place?

With a 4-20 mA signal, only 800 out of the 1000 A/D converter units are usable. The temperature range covers 90°C, so you have: 800 * X = 90, meaning X = 0.1125. To span the 90°C range, multiply the 800 units by 0.1125. However, the analog amplifier only accepts values with up to 2 decimal places, so you could only use 0.11 or 0.12, which would distort the result. Therefore, the scaling is done in two stages: first, multiply by 1.25 to convert 800 units to 1000; then multiply by 0.09 so 1000 units become 90. 1.25 * 0.09 = 0.1125. For a decimal place, set the second amplifier’s gain to 0.9, Min to -300, Max to 600, and OFFSET to -300.

Hello! I'm new here and seeking assistance. I've searched online but haven't found a solution to my problem. I'm using a [product_name] with an [product_name] expansion and have connected a three-wire PT100 sensor according to diagrams from [company_name] and the probe manufacturer. My program is simple; I just want to display the temperature on an [product_name] display for now. I'm using an analog amplifier set to PT100/PT1000 with 0.1 resolution and have configured the message text to show one decimal place. Everything seems to be functioning, but when testing, I notice the temperature jumps in 0.3 degree increments and doesn't show the values in between. Am I missing something? Thanks in advance for any help!

The issue is caused by the limited 10-bit resolution of the analog inputs in [product_name]. The A/D converter turns any input (whether voltage, current, or PT100/1000) into 0–1000 units. The [product_name] expansion sets a temperature range from -50 to 200 °C, so the resolution becomes 0.25°C per unit (250/1000 = 0.25). As [product_name]'s system uses integer values only (not float or real values), decimal places aren't truly processed—it's just for display formatting. Selecting 0.1 resolution for PT100/PT1000 only alters how many decimal places are shown in the message text, not the actual measurable resolution. For resolution 1 with no decimal place selected, the text will show values from -50 to 200 °C, updating by 4 units per 1°C, and the system rounds the value. For 0.1 resolution with one decimal displayed, the text shows -50.0 to 200.0 °C, updating by 1 unit per 0.25°C, but again rounding occurs. Examples: At 0.1 resolution, readings go like 0.0, 0.3, 0.5, 0.8, 1.0, 1.3, showing jumps of 0.2°C or 0.3°C when the unit changes.

It's helpful to use the simulation feature to better understand how this operates.

A suggestion: The "Average value" block in [product_name] may make the displayed temperature appear smoother, though it doesn't improve measurement precision.

After removing the component, the controller powers up without issues. It was a small, unmarked surface-mount part, roughly 1mm square. Once I took it out, it got lost—probably somewhere in the carpet under my desk.

The part is likely a crowbar diode, positioned in parallel across the input to protect against over- or reverse-voltage by shorting. Using the [product_name] without it is possible, but adding a new one will restore the protection.

For all versions rated at 230 Volts, I always add an extra 275MOV directly onto the terminals. In the event of overvoltage, it activates first and blows the fuse. This method works well when the power supply isn't stable, such as when using heavily loaded or misused generators. It's easy to explain to the customer: just reset the fuse; if that doesn't work, replace the 275MOV. These have consistently protected my [product_name] devices. Previously, I saw many burned power supplies from [product_name]. In my home, I use 12 programmable controllers and live in an area prone to lightning strikes. One of my controllers starts the generator during outages (which happen multiple times a year), and thanks to my protection setup, I haven't lost a controller—even after several strikes, although a generator was lost due to a nearby strike.
